claim: In Shirazi et al. (2014), 42 male rats weighing 180±20 g were randomly divided into six groups of seven animals each; partial urethral obstruction (PUO) was induced by opening the abdominal cavity via a midline incision to reach the posterior urethra, introducing a pediatric 22-gauge Angiocath to the posterior urethra, tying a silk 4-0 ligature around the Angiocath, and then removing the Angiocath to induce PUO. source_text:
This study was conducted on 42 male rats weighing  $180 \pm 20$  g. ... The rats were randomly divided into six groups each including seven animals... The sham-operated animals underwent laparotomy only without undergoing any procedures or receiving any treatments. Other groups, however, underwent a surgery to induce PUO.

After the rats were anesthetized with ketamine/xylazine ... the abdominal cavity was opened by a midline incision to reach the posterior urethra. Then, a pediatric 22-gauge Angiocath was introduced to the posterior urethra and a silk 4-0 ligature was tied around the Angiocath. Afterwards, the Angiocath was removed and PUO was induced.

claim: In male Sprague–Dawley rats, partial bladder outlet obstruction was induced under ketamine/xylazine anesthesia via a low midline abdominal incision to enter the pelvic cavity, with distal retraction of the prostate, removal of perivesical fat at the level of the bladder neck, circumferential dissection of the prostatic urethra, and passage of a 2–0 silk suture between the urethra and rectum at the level of the bladder neck; the urethra was tightened by tying the silk over a pre-placed 1-mm intraurethral catheter to reduce urethral diameter to nearly 2/3 of original size and prevent complete obstruction, then the catheter was removed and the abdominal incision closed in layers. Sham rats underwent general anesthesia and abdominal exploration without urinary tract intervention.
source_text: “General anesthesia was induced with intramuscular injections of ketamine (44 mg/kg) and xylazine (8 mg/kg). Before the operation, the animals received a single intramuscular injection of gentamicin (1 mg/kg) to prevent infection. Through a low midline abdominal incision, the pelvic cavity was entered. After distal retraction of the prostate, removal of the perivesical fat at the level of the bladder neck, and circumferential dissection of the prostatic urethra, a 2–0 Silk suture was passed between the urethra and rectum at the level of bladder neck. By tying the 2–0 silk material, the urethra was tightened over a pre-placed 1-mm intraurethral catheter. The catheter was placed to reduce the urethral diameter to nearly 2/3 of its original size and to prevent complete obstruction of the urethra. After removing the catheter, the abdominal incision was closed in layers. The rats in the sham group only underwent general anesthesia and abdominal exploration without any intervention on their urinary tract.”
verdict_explanation: The source supports the low midline abdominal incision, dissection at bladder neck/prostatic urethra, 2–0 silk tie over a pre-placed 1-mm intraurethral catheter, the purpose/extent of narrowing (nearly 2/3) to prevent complete obstruction, catheter removal, layered closure, and sham anesthesia + abdominal exploration without urinary tract intervention. readiness_reason: Repaired claim is directly and specifically supported by verbatim surgical-technique text, with clear animal model context and sham description.

claim: In this rat partial-BOO model at 4 weeks, mean bladder weight was significantly higher in BOO animals than sham (P<0.001), and there was no statistically significant difference in bladder weight between BOO+PTX and BOO control.

claim: The authors state mechanistically that PTX, as an inhibitor of phosphodiesterase and activator of nitric oxide (NO) synthase, increases tissue NO and intracellular cGMP (presented as mechanisms that can describe PTX’s beneficial effects after ischemic injury).
source_text: “PTX is a potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant agent. As an inhibitor of phosphodiesterase and activator of nitric oxide (NO) synthase, PTX increases the level of tissue NO and intracellular cGMP. These mechanisms can describe the promising effect of PTX on improvement of contractile abilities of cardiac papillary muscles after ischemic injury [6].”
verdict_explanation: Supported in Discussion as proposed/explanatory mechanisms: PDE inhibition + NO synthase activation with increased NO/cGMP; anti-fibrotic effects framed via VEGF up and TGFβ1 down; and the inference from electrical stimulation vs carbachol dissociation leading to an assumption of non-cholinergic (purinergic or other NANC) pathways. However, the candidate claim adds an additional proposed mechanism—“protection of microvascular perfusion against cyclic ischemia–reperfusion injury”—that is not explicitly proposed as a mechanism of PTX’s effect in the Discussion (the Discussion describes ischemia/reperfusion and perfusion issues generally, but does not explicitly attribute PTX’s effect to protecting microvascular perfusion against cyclic ischemia–reperfusion injury).
readiness_reason: Directly stated as mechanism in Discussion; faithful compression possible.
original_claim: The authors propose that because PTX improved electrically evoked (nerve-mediated) contractions without improving carbachol-evoked contractions, PTX may protect non-cholinergic (e.g., purinergic/NANC) neuro-effector transmission rather than post-synaptic muscarinic receptor function, potentially via phosphodiesterase inhibition with effects on NO/cGMP signaling, anti-inflammatory/anti-fibrotic effects (e.g., reduced pro-fibrotic cytokines such as TGF-β1), and/or protection of microvascular perfusion against cyclic ischemia–reperfusion injury.

claim: In a retrospective chart review of patients seen by benign urologists at one ambulatory clinic from April 2022 to September 2022, 120 patients were referred to PFPT; the flowchart reports 73 (60.8%) scheduled an appointment, 46 (~38.3%) did not schedule, and 1 (0.83%) was scheduled outside a 6-month window. In the RESULTS text, 74 (8.1% of total, 62% of referred) were scheduled. Among those who scheduled, 52 attended, 14 cancelled, and 8 were no-shows. The CONCLUSIONS state that approximately 1/12 patients are referred to pelvic floor PT.
source_text:
**METHODS:** This was a retrospective chart review of patients seen by benign urologists at one of our ambulatory clinics from April 2022 to September 2022 using ICD codes for BPH, OAB, LUTS, CP/CPPS, Pelvic Pain/PFD, Chronic Bladder Pain and Urinary Urgency.

**RESULTS:** 74 (8.1% of total, 62% of referred) were subsequently scheduled for a PT appointment. Of the patients who scheduled an appointment, 52(5.7% of total, 70.3% of scheduled) attended their

appointment, 14 patients cancelled their appointment (1.5% of total, 18.9% of scheduled), and 8 patients were a ‘no show’ (0.9% of total, 10.8% of scheduled). Only 1 patient (0.11% of total, 0.83% of scheduled) was scheduled outside of a 6-month window. The mean wait time between referral and appointment was 54.7 days (SD=37.3, Range=1-215).

CONCLUSIONS: At our institution, approximately 1/12 patients are referred to pelvic floor PT and over half of referred patients follow through with at least one therapy visit. Barriers to therapy include low referral rates, long wait times for therapy appointments, and difficulties for patients to complete scheduled appointments due to cancellations and no-shows.

Blood was immediately centrifuged and plasma was kept at  $-20^{\circ}\text{C}$  until analyzed.

claim: Kaplan et al. state that pseudodyssynergia (in contrast to neurologic detrusor-external sphincter dyssynergia) is secondary to voluntary contraction of the external sphincter, including voluntary increases in sphincteric activity during attempted inhibition of an involuntary detrusor contraction, abdominal straining, or discomfort during voiding.
source_text: "The term pseudodyssynergia is used in contrast to the more commonly described detrusor-external sphincter dyssynergia. The etiology of detrusor-external sphincter dyssynergia, or involuntary detrusor contractions concomitant with involuntary contraction of or inability to relax the external sphincter, is neurological (that is patients with spinal cord injury). In contrast, pseudodyssynergia is secondary to voluntary contraction of the external sphincter and includes voluntary increases in sphincteric activity during attempted inhibition of an involuntary detrusor contraction, abdominal straining or discomfort during voiding."
verdict_explanation: The source supports: (a) pseudodyssynergia being secondary to voluntary external sphincter contraction (as contrasted with neurologic DSD); (b) diagnostic criteria including external sphincter electrical activity during voiding in the absence of abdominal straining; (c) brief/intermittent closing of the membranous urethra during voiding detected on EMG and fluoroscopy; (d) private-setting uroflowmetry with an undulating flow pattern intended to reduce false positives from performance anxiety/"bashful voiding"; and (e) exclusion of patients with positive bacterial culture or excessive leukocytes in expressed prostatic secretions (>10 WBC). Not supported as written: defining pseudodyssynergia as 'functional bladder outlet obstruction' (that phrasing appears as a conclusion about misdiagnosed patients, not as the definition), EMG described as 'persistent or increased activity during detrusor contraction in the voiding phase', fluoroscopy described as 'persistent narrowing or cutoff' (only brief/intermittent closing/cutoff is described), and 'negative urine/prostatic cultures' framed as a diagnostic criterion rather than an exclusion rule.
readiness_reason: Direct definitional/etiologic statement with exact wording supported in the source.
original_claim: Kaplan et al. (1997) define pseudodyssynergia as functional bladder outlet obstruction caused by voluntary/dysfunctional contraction of the striated external urinary sphincter during micturition, and diagnose it using multimodal criteria including: (i) external urethral sphincter EMG showing persistent or increased activity during detrusor contraction in the voiding phase (in the absence of abdominal straining), (ii) fluoroscopic video-cystourethrography showing brief/intermittent/persistent narrowing or cutoff at the membranous urethra during attempted voiding, (iii) private-room uroflowmetry demonstrating an undulating/fluctuating flow curve (used to reduce false positives from performance anxiety during formal testing), and (iv) negative urine/prostatic cultures and no excessive leukocytes in expressed prostatic secretions.

verdict_explanation: All mean±SD baseline measures (AUA symptom score 17.5±3.7; maximum flow rate 13.3±4.2 ml/s; detrusor pressure at maximum flow 46.3±13.7 cm water; detrusor contraction duration 132.8±27.7 s) and all categorical counts/percents (detrusor instability 17/43 [40%]; bladder outlet obstruction 30/43 [70%]; impaired detrusor contractility 13/43 [30%]; acontractile 0/43 [0%]) are explicitly reported in ABSTRACT and/or RESULTS. original_claim: Kaplan et al. (1997) report baseline measures in the 43 men including AUA symptom score 17.5±3.7, Qmax 13.3±4.2 mL/s, Pdet at Qmax 46.3±13.7 cm H2O, and detrusor contraction duration 132.8±27.7 s; they also classify urodynamics as detrusor instability in 17/43 (40%), bladder outlet obstruction in 30/43 (70%), impaired detrusor contractility in 13/43 (30%), and acontractile detrusor in 0/43 (0%). The study’s operational thresholds include: detrusor instability as nonvolitional phasic detrusor pressure rise ≥15 cm H2O (or associated with uninhibited urgency), bladder outlet obstruction requiring sustained detrusor contraction >45 cm H2O with catheterized max flow <12 mL/s plus radiographic urethral narrowing, impaired detrusor contractility defined by peak detrusor pressure <30 cm H2O with catheterized flow <12 mL/s (or low pressure/low flow with Pdet 30–45 cm H2O and flow <12), and pathologic detrusor contraction duration defined as >120 seconds.

claim: Kaplan et al. report that men with pseudodyssynergia were treated with behavior modification and external sphincter EMG biofeedback using the Incare PRS 8900 unit; each session lasted 20–30 minutes, occurred once or twice weekly, and could be done intermittently for several weeks. Success was defined a priori as at least a 50% decrease in symptoms on 2 consecutive office visits. They report that 35 of 43 patients (83%) achieved a 50% symptom decrease by 3 months (with AUA symptom scores in these men decreasing from 18.4 at baseline to 7.6 at 3 months and 8.1 at 6 months). The Abstract instead states the 83% figure at 6 months, creating an internal discrepancy in timepoint attribution.
source_text:
Biofeedback training with the Incare PRS 8900* unit was used to treat the men. Therapy was designed to teach patients to recognize and correct pelvic floor contraction during voiding. Biofeedback was performed by instructing patients to relax the pelvic floor muscles during voiding. Patients were shown the activity during resting and voiding, and essentially instructed to mimic sphincteric activity demonstrated during the relaxation phase throughout the voiding cycle. The patient visually monitored muscle activity of the contraction and relaxation phases during treatment. Each session lasted 20 to 30 minutes, occurred once or twice a week and could be done intermittently for several weeks. Success was defined as a decrease in symptoms of at least 50% on 2 consecutive office visits.

Behavior modification and biofeedback were successful in decreasing symptoms by 50% in 35 patients (83%) at 3 months. For these men AUA symptom scores decreased from 18.4 to 7.6 and 8.1 at 3 and 6 months, respectively.

citation.locator: ## Diagnostic aspects > ### Detrusor contraction strength > #### 2. Projected isovolumetric pressure (PIP)

claim: Osman et al. describe Schäfer’s projected isovolumetric pressure (PIP) as PIP = pdet@Qmax + K·Qmax, where K depends on population and differs between men and women; in men it is usually taken as 5. They list suggested PIP contractility groupings (>150 strong; 100 to 150 normal; 50 to 100 weak; <50 very weak). They also state that reported PIP variants include the bladder contractility index (BCI), described as essentially the same as PIP but with different groupings, and that these formulae may overestimate PIP and have less test-retest reliability than measuring isovolumetric pressures directly.
source_text:
The PIP was proposed by Schäfer, who used a straight line to represent the BOR and then “projected” back to the y-axis ( $p_{det}$ ) from the point representing  $p_{det@Q_{max}}$  to obtain the isovolumetric pressure. This projection is calculated by the formula  $PIP = p_{det@Q_{max}} + KQ_{max}$  where  $K$  is a fixed constant representing the steepness of the angle of the BOR to x-a axis<sup>28</sup>.  $K$  is dependent on the specific population studied and differs between men and women<sup>29</sup>; in men it is usually taken as 5. The suggested groupings for PIP are as follows:

- >150 – strong contractility
- 100 to 150 – normal contractility
- 50 to 100 – weak contractility
- <50 – very weak contractility

There are two other reported variants of the PIP: the detrusor coefficient (DECO), which is the PIP divided by 100, and the bladder contractility index (BCI), which is essentially the same as PIP but with different groupings. The main advantage with these formulae is that they are easy and quick to use; however, they may overestimate PIP and have less test-retest reliability than measuring isovolumetric pressures directly<sup>30</sup>.
verdict_explanation: Supported: PIP formula; statement that K differs by population and sex and is usually 5 in men; the four PIP contractility cutoffs; mention of BCI as a variant and the limitation statement that these formulae may overestimate PIP and have less test–retest reliability than direct isovolumetric measurement. Not supported in this source: the candidate’s explicit equation for BCI ("BCI = pdet@Qmax + 5·Qmax") and the cutoff "BCI<100" defining detrusor underactivity; the text only says BCI is essentially the same as PIP but with different groupings, without giving the BCI formula or thresholds.
readiness_reason: After removing unsupported specifics (BCI formula and BCI<100 cutoff), the remaining claim is directly and fully supported by the quoted PIP section.
original_claim: Osman et al. describe Schäfer’s projected isovolumetric pressure (PIP = pdet@Qmax + K·Qmax, with K typically 5 in men) with contractility categories (>150 cmH2O strong; 100–150 normal; 50–100 weak; <50 very weak) and note a related variant, the bladder contractility index (BCI = pdet@Qmax + 5·Qmax) with BCI<100 defining detrusor underactivity; they state PIP/BCI tend to overestimate true isovolumetric pressure and have lower test–retest reliability than direct mechanical isovolumetric occlusion.

source_text: This projection is calculated by the formula  $PIP = p_{det@Q_{max}} + KQ_{max}$  where  $K$  is a fixed constant representing the steepness of the angle of the BOR to x-a axis<sup>28</sup>.  $K$  is dependent on the specific population studied and differs between men and women<sup>29</sup>; in men it is usually taken as 5.
verdict_explanation: Supported: PIP formula; statement that K differs by population and sex and is usually 5 in men; the four PIP contractility cutoffs; mention of BCI as a variant and the limitation statement that these formulae may overestimate PIP and have less test–retest reliability than direct isovolumetric measurement. Not supported in this source: the candidate’s explicit equation for BCI ("BCI = pdet@Qmax + 5·Qmax") and the cutoff "BCI<100" defining detrusor underactivity; the text only says BCI is essentially the same as PIP but with different groupings, without giving the BCI formula or thresholds.
readiness_reason: Exact formula and qualifier statements are explicitly present in the source text.
original_claim: Osman et al. describe Schäfer’s projected isovolumetric pressure (PIP = pdet@Qmax + K·Qmax, with K typically 5 in men) with contractility categories (>150 cmH2O strong; 100–150 normal; 50–100 weak; <50 very weak) and note a related variant, the bladder contractility index (BCI = pdet@Qmax + 5·Qmax) with BCI<100 defining detrusor underactivity; they state PIP/BCI tend to overestimate true isovolumetric pressure and have lower test–retest reliability than direct mechanical isovolumetric occlusion.

claim: In this porcine model of haemorrhage plus peritonitis, pentoxifylline given simultaneously with colloid resuscitation reduced systemic/pulmonary vascular resistance and worsened the hypotension associated with ‘septic shock’.
source_text: “In summary, it has been shown that, when given simultaneously with a colloid regimen during the resuscitation from the combined insults of haemorrhage and infection, pentoxifylline reduced vascular resistance and worsened the hypotension associated with ‘septic shock’.”
verdict_explanation: The source supports that PTX reduced SVRI/PVRI (vasodilatory effect) and worsened hypotension during resuscitation, and the authors interpret lactic acidosis as probably from reduced tissue perfusion/cellular hypoxia (mechanistic interpretation). However, the candidate adds unsupported specifics: (1) 'given concurrently with volume resuscitation in established septic shock'—the paper discusses hypotension associated with septic shock, and compares to other models where shock was established, but does not explicitly frame their intervention as occurring in 'established septic shock' as a key attribution in that clause; (2) 'uncompensated drop'—not stated; (3) 'compromised organ perfusion/microvascular flow distribution (tissue dysoxia)'—the paper says reduced tissue perfusion/cellular hypoxia and says unlikely to improve perfusion/oxygen delivery, but does not mention microvascular flow distribution or tissue dysoxia; (4) 'exceeded a non-hypotensive therapeutic threshold'—the paper calls the regimen 'high-dose' and discusses a 'therapeutic window' reported by Ridings et al., but does not define or claim their regimen exceeded a specific non-hypotensive threshold/therapeutic threshold in swine.
readiness_reason: Directly stated summary of observed preclinical effects in this study; attribution and scope are explicit.
original_claim: The authors argue that pentoxifylline’s phosphodiesterase-inhibitory vasodilatory effects, when given concurrently with volume resuscitation in established septic shock, caused an uncompensated drop in vascular resistance and arterial hypotension that compromised organ perfusion/microvascular flow distribution (tissue dysoxia), and that the regimen used (20 mg/kg bolus plus 20 mg/kg/h infusion) exceeded a non-hypotensive therapeutic threshold in swine with septic shock.

citation.locator: ### Combination Therapy

claim: In the “Combination Therapy” section, Bortnick et al. (2019) reports that the MTOPS trial (3047 men; average age 62.6 years [SD 7.3]) found finasteride+doxazosin improved voiding symptoms and maximum urinary flow rate more than either agent alone, and that MTOPS showed combination therapy prevented BPH progression better than either agent alone and reduced long-term risk of acute urinary retention and need for invasive therapy. The review further reports that these results were confirmed in the CombAT trial (men >50 with symptomatic BPH; 58% of patients were >65 years), in which combination dutasteride+tamsulosin had greater risk reduction in acute urinary retention or BPH-related surgery and greater reduction in relative risk of clinical progression than either monotherapy. (The review does not state CombAT enrolled 4,844 men.)
source_text: The medical therapy of prostate symptoms (MTOPS) trial studied the combination of finasteride (alpha-blocker) with doxazosin (5-alpha reductase inhibitor) in 3047 men with average age 62.6 years (SD 7.3 years) and found that the combination improved voiding symptoms and maximum urinary flow rate more than either agent alone. MTOPS also showed that combination therapy prevented the progression of BPH better than either agent alone and reduced the long-term risk of acute urinary retention and need for invasive therapy [21]. These results were confirmed in the CombAT (Combination of Avodart and Tamsulosin) trial, a multicenter, randomized, double-blind study in men over 50 years old with symptomatic BPH comparing the combination of tamsulosin and dutasteride to either agent alone. Fifty-eight percent of the patients were over 65 years old. Combination therapy had greater risk reduction in acute urinary retention or BPH-related surgery and greater reduction in the relative risk of clinical progression than either agent monotherapy [22].
verdict_explanation: Supported: the review attributes to MTOPS that combination therapy was superior to either agent alone for improving voiding symptoms and maximum urinary flow rate, preventing BPH progression, and reducing long-term risk of acute urinary retention and need for invasive therapy; it explicitly states MTOPS enrolled 3047 men. Supported: it reports CombAT confirmed these results and states 58% of patients were >65, and that combination therapy had greater risk reduction in AUR or BPH-related surgery and greater reduction in relative risk of clinical progression than either monotherapy. Not supported: the review text provided does not state CombAT enrolled 4,844 men (that number is not present in the supplied source). Also, the MTOPS parenthetical drug-class mapping appears internally reversed in the source text (finasteride labeled “alpha-blocker” and doxazosin labeled “5-alpha reductase inhibitor”), but this FRD only verifies what Bortnick et al. wrote, not external correctness.
readiness_reason: After removing the unsupported CombAT enrollment number (4,844), the remaining statements are directly supported by exact quoted text in the specified section, with clear attribution to the review’s reporting of MTOPS and CombAT outcomes and MTOPS sample size / CombAT age distribution.
original_claim: Bortnick et al. (2019) summarizes MTOPS and CombAT as showing combination therapy (alpha-blocker + 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor) is superior to either monotherapy for preventing BPH clinical progression and reducing long-term risk of acute urinary retention and need for invasive BPH surgery; it notes MTOPS enrolled 3,047 men and CombAT enrolled 4,844 men (58% >65 years).

claim: Hall et al. (2018) report substantial heterogeneity in male PFMT program content and reporting across 108 included studies; the intensity of programs ranged from 18 to 240 pelvic floor muscle contractions per day, and when hold times were reported for home exercise programs the most common hold time was 10 seconds. They also report that the anal sphincter was most commonly identified as the intervention focus (n=44 studies), only 7% (n=8/108) focused specifically on urethral pressure, and 21 studies encompassed both anal and urinary regions.
source_text:
**Results:** Results from the 108 included studies indicate substantial heterogeneity in both the content of PFMT and the quality of reporting of the components of the exercise regimes. There was notable disparity in the muscles targeted by the interventions (and few focused on urethral control despite the use in management of urinary conditions) and the intensity of the programs (eg, 18–240 contractions per day). ...

The anal sphincter was the region of the pelvic floor most commonly identified as the focus of the intervention ( $n=44$ ). Given the majority of studies involved an UI indication, surprisingly only 7% ( $n=8$ ) focused their training specifically on instructions related to urethral pressure. Instructions and feedback that encompassed both the anal and urinary regions were identified in 21 included studies (Figure 3E).

Contractions per day ranged from 18 to 240 with 50-51 daily contractions the most common ( $n=9$ ) (Figure 4C). ... In most instances, the hold and relax times were not provided ( $n=60$  and  $n=69$ , respectively) but when they were, the most common time for both was 10 s ( $n=10$  and  $n=12$ , respectively) (Figures 5A and 5B).
verdict_explanation: Supported: contraction/day range (18–240), anal-focus count (n=44), urethral-focus percentage and count (7%; n=8 of 108), and both-region count (21). Not supported as written: the candidate claim adds that interventions were "predominantly strengthening-focused" and that they "commonly prescrib[ed] repetitive maximal or submaximal" contractions with "2–10 second holds" as a general prescription pattern. The source excerpt does mention intensity descriptors (eg, “Maximal,” “firm,” etc.) in 13 studies and reports hold times, including that 10 s was most common when reported; it does not state that the overall interventions were predominantly strengthening-focused, nor that 2–10 s holds were commonly prescribed overall (2–10 s appears in some individual studies/tables but is not summarized in the Results text as the common hold-time range). Therefore the claim required narrowing to what is explicitly reported in the supplied source text.
readiness_reason: The repaired claim is directly supported by verbatim passages in the supplied excerpts, with clear study counts and ranges that can be faithfully witness-constructed.

claim: In this review, the authors state that alpha-blockers commonly cause dizziness and orthostatic hypotension, which are of increased concern in the elderly because they can lead to falls and injuries; they also state that alpha-blockers are associated with intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS), which can increase cataract surgery complications, and they recommend screening for potential cataract surgery and consultation with an ophthalmologist before starting alpha-blockers. The authors further summarize two cohort studies on dementia: (1) Duan et al. used Medicare data (2006–2012) in >250,000 males >65 with BPH and reported significantly higher dementia risk with tamsulosin compared with no BPH medication or several alternative BPH medications; (2) Tae et al. used the Korean National Health Insurance Service database in 59,263 patients >70 with BPH and found no significant difference in dementia incidence for tamsulosin compared with doxazosin, alfuzosin, or no medication (including after propensity score matching).
source_text:
Common side effects of these medications include dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, retrograde ejaculation, and rhinitis. Dizziness and orthostatic hypotension are of increased concern in the elderly population as they can lead to significant morbidity, such as falls and subsequent injuries. Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS), a sudden intraoperative iris prolapse and pupil constriction, is also a major concern for patient on these medications. IFIS can increase the risk of complications during cataract surgery. Although increased age has not been found to be associated with increased risk of IFIS, it is important to screen patients who potentially will be undergoing cataract surgery. It is recommended that they consult an ophthalmologist before starting alpha-blockers so as to avoid any surgical complications.

Concerns have emerged regarding the risk of development of dementia in patients who are taking alpha-blockers. ... In order to explore the relationship between risk of dementia with tamsulosin use and other medical therapies for BPH, Duan et al. conducted a cohort study in over 250,000 males. Included patients were >65 years of age with a diagnosis of BPH in Medicare data from 2006 to 2012, based on patient charts with ICD-9 diagnostic codes for dementia. With a mean follow up of 19.8 months, the risk of dementia was found to be significantly higher in older men with BPH taking tamsulosin in comparison with men who did not take any other BPH medications or to those who take doxazosin, terazosin, alfuzosin, dutasteride, or finasteride.

However, a recent article by Tae et al. disputes this study. Using the National Health Insurance Service database from Korea, 59,263 patients >70 years old with BPH were studied to compare those taking tamsulosin with those taking doxazosin, terazosin, alfuzosin, and no medication with the incidence of dementia. After a mean follow up of 1580 days (about 52.6 months), no significant difference was seen in the incidence of dementia in the tamsulosin cohort compared with doxazosin, alfuzosin, or no medication. This remained true after propensity score matching for the drug cohorts, and, thus, the authors concluded that BPH medication is not associated with risk of dementia.

claim: In a preliminary trial in normal rats (without endotoxemia), an intravenous aminophylline loading dose of 6 mg/kg followed by 1 mg/kg/h maintenance in four rats decreased arterial Hb-O2 saturation to 40–45% and was associated with cardiac arrhythmias, metabolic acidosis, excessive urination, and death in 3/4 rats before the end of the 6-h experiment; a 3 mg/kg bolus followed by 1 mg/kg/h in two rats led to death in 1/2 rats at 3 h; therefore, for the present study the authors used 1 mg/kg bolus followed by 0.5 mg/kg/h as a regimen that proved safe.
source_text: In a preliminary trial, we studied the safe amount of aminophylline to be administered intravenously for both the loading and maintenance doses in normal rats. Administration of an aminophylline loading dose of 6 mg/kg followed by a maintenance dose of 1 mg/kg/h in four rats led to significant decreases in the arterial Hb-O2 saturation (HbO2 of 40–45%). These rats developed cardiac arrhythmias, metabolic acidosis, and excessive urination. This was followed by death in three of the four rats prior to the end of the 6-h experimental period. A bolus of 3 mg/kg aminophylline, followed by a maintenance dose of 1 mg/kg/h in two rats also proved relatively unsafe, with one of the two rats expiring 3 h after injection. Therefore, in the present study, Groups I and III received a bolus of 1 mg/kg aminophylline followed by a maintenance dose of 0.5 mg/kg/h which proved to be safe.

claim: In a 12-week double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial in 60 medically stable outpatients with major depression (treatment-resistant), participants received infliximab 5 mg/kg (n=30) or placebo (n=30) as 3 IV infusions at baseline and weeks 2 and 6. In the intent-to-treat mixed-effects model for repeated measures, there was no difference in change in HAM-D scores over time between treatment groups (t58=0.10, P=.92) and no significant treatment×time interaction (t305=0.86, P=.39). When baseline hs-CRP (log-linear and quadratic terms) was entered, there was a significant interaction among treatment, time, and log hs-CRP (t302=2.65, P=.01). The paper reports that infliximab began to favorably outperform placebo at plasma hs-CRP concentrations greater than 4.98 mg/L (described in text as >5 mg/L).
source_text:
**Participants:** A total of 60 medically stable outpatients with major depression ...

**Interventions:** Three infusions of the TNF antagonist infliximab (5 mg/kg) (n=30) or placebo (n=30) at baseline and weeks 2 and 6 of a 12-week trial.

... Following screening for inclusion and exclusion criteria, all participants reported to the infusion center ... on 3 separate occasions (baseline, 2 weeks, and 6 weeks) to receive an infusion of either infliximab (5 mg/kg) or placebo over 120 minutes through an indwelling catheter.

No differences in change in HAM-D scores over time were found between treatment groups ( $t_{58} = 0.10, P = .92$ ), nor was there a significant interaction between treatment and time ( $t_{305} = 0.86, P = .39$ ) (**Figure 1**). ... Interestingly, when the baseline hs-CRP concentration (log-linear and quadratic terms) was entered into the model, there was a significant interaction among treatment, time, and log hs-CRP concentration ( $t_{302} = 2.65, P = .01$ ). To identify the critical threshold for the influence of baseline hs-CRP concentration, we examined change in HAM-D from baseline to week 12 (infliximab minus placebo) in relation to log hs-CRP concentration. A baseline hs-CRP concentration greater than 5 mg/L was found to be the point at which infliximab-treated patients began to exhibit a greater decrease in HAM-D scores than placebo-treated patients (**Figure 2**).

**Figure 2.** ... At plasma hs-CRP concentrations greater than 4.98 mg/L, the change in HAM-D scores favored infliximab-treated patients, whereas at plasma hs-CRP concentrations below 4.98 mg/L, the change in HAM-D scores favored placebo-treated patients.

Minor repair: the claim says 'IV (weeks 0, 2, 6)' which is consistent with 'baseline and weeks 2 and 6' and 'receive an infusion ... through an indwelling catheter', but the source does not explicitly state 'IV' in the Interventions line (it does say 'intravenous administration' elsewhere and describes infusion via catheter).
readiness_reason: Claim is directly supported with exact dosing/schedule/sample size and the specified t statistics/df and P values, plus explicit wording for the hs-CRP threshold (5 mg/L and 4.98 mg/L in Figure 2 caption).

claim: Xiao et al. source_text:
“The study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. First, as a retrospective case–control study, it is subject to selection bias and confounding variables, despite our efforts to match groups on baseline characteristics. The significant differences in education level and hypertension prevalence between groups could have influenced outcomes. Second, the follow-up period of 6 months may be insufficient to assess the long-term sustainability of the observed benefits. Future studies with longitudinal designs are needed to determine whether the improvements persist over time and whether quality of life differences emerge with longer follow-up.

Third, the use of self-reported measures for psychological assessments introduces the potential for response bias. Fourth, our sample was drawn from a single institution, which may limit the generalizability of findings to diverse populations with varying healthcare practices and resources. Finally, the absence of a structured protocol for measuring adherence to the exercise regimen limits our ability to establish a dose–response relationship between exercise compliance and outcomes.”
verdict_explanation: The candidate claim closely matches the Discussion’s explicit limitation statements about (1) lack of a structured adherence-measurement protocol limiting ability to establish a dose–response relationship and (2) single-institution sampling limiting generalizability to diverse populations with different practices/resources. In experiments for PTX effect, the animals received PTX (30 mg/kg, i.v.) 10 min before the reflow of blood. The control animals untreated with the drug received an equal volume of saline.

Table 1 summarizes changes in renal function in rabbits with ischemic acute renal failure treated and untreated with PTX. ... The PTX pretreatment significantly reduced the levels of serum creatinine and BUN after renal ischemia. PTX also attenuated the reduction of GFR in postischemic kidney.

**Table 1.** Effect of Pentoxifylline (PTX) on Renal Function in Rabbits with Ischemic Acute Renal Failure

| Parameters          | Periods      | – PTX           | + PTX           |
|---------------------|--------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Pcr (mg/dL)         | Basal        | 0.82 ± 0.12     | 0.76 ± 0.15     |
|                     | Postischemic | 3.20 ± 0.34*    | 1.99 ± 0.21*#   |
| BUN (mg/dL)         | Basal        | 46.68 ± 7.38    | 46.36 ± 6.26    |
|                     | Postischemic | 146.84 ± 15.04* | 92.06 ± 14.82*# |
| GFR (L/day/kg)      | Basal        | 2.34 ± 0.18     | 2.46 ± 0.03     |
|                     | Postischemic | 0.09 ± 0.30*    | 0.33 ± 0.06*#   |

Renal function was measured for 24 h before ischemia (basal period) and for 24 h of reperfusion following 60 min of ischemia (postischemic period) in rabbits treated and untreated with PTX. The animals received PTX (+PTX, 30 mg/kg, i.v.) or an equal volume of saline (– PTX) 10 min before reperfusion of blood. Data are mean ± SEM of nine animals in each group. \**p* < 0.05 compared with basal period; #*p* < 0.05 compared with the respective – PTX group.

The original claim’s phrasing “single IV bolus” is not explicitly stated in the source (source says “received PTX (30 mg/kg, i.v.) 10 min before the reflow of blood”); the remainder, including the significance notation (* vs basal; # vs –PTX, both p<0.05), is directly supported.

claim: In a two-occasion (within-subject) study of 10 healthy male volunteers given 100 ng LPS (sodium salt of LPS from Salmonella abortus equi) IV at 8:00 a.m., an IV infusion of pentoxifylline (POF) 500 mg in 500 ml isotonic saline started 30 minutes before endotoxin and continued for 4 hours (vs isotonic saline infusion 125 ml/h on the other occasion) prevented the endotoxin-induced rise in serum TNF (max at 2 h post-endotoxin without POF; TNF levels 2 h were significantly different between treatment with and without POF; Fig. 4 shows baseline TNF 20 pg/ml in both conditions and 2 h values of ~38 pg/ml without POF vs ~23 pg/ml with POF). POF did not affect IL-6 levels after endotoxin administration, did not affect endotoxin-induced cortisol changes, and did not affect the clinical responses to endotoxin (fever/heart rate increase; symptoms such as myalgia, headache, nausea; blood pressure unaffected).
source_text:
Ten male volunteers (26–38 years old), each of whom had given informed consent before joining the study, were treated with endotoxin and examined on two occasions separated by at least 21 days: endotoxin preparation (sodium salt of LPS from *Salmonella abortus equi*) was dissolved in isotonic saline and given as a bolus injection (100 ng) intravenously at 8.00 a.m. An intravenous infusion of isotonic saline (125 ml/h) on the first occasion or POF (500 mg in 500 ml isotonic saline) on the second occasion was started 30 min before endotoxin administration and continued for 4 h.

In nine of ten subjects there was a rise in body temperature of at least 1.0°C, paralleled by an increase in heart rate. ... Eight of the remaining nine subjects responded to endotoxin with symptoms such as myalgia and headache, which started 70–100 min after the injection. Two subjects also had nausea (120 min after endotoxin). Systolic and diastolic blood pressure were not affected. None of the clinical responses to endotoxin were affected by POF.

Circulating TNF levels were determined in sera sampled over short time intervals. It was found that a maximum serum level was reached 2 h postendotoxin (Fig. 4). This increase was statistically significant. ... When POF was infused, no increase in TNF levels was observed (Fig. 4).

| Time after LPS-injection (h) | LPS (pg/ml) | LPS + POF (pg/ml) |
|------------------------------|-------------|-------------------|
| -1                           | 20          | 20                |
| 0                            | 20          | 22                |
| 1                            | 30          | 23                |
| 2                            | 38          | 23                |
| 3                            | 22          | 20                |
| 4                            | 18          | 19                |
| 7                            | 19          | 20                |

**Fig. 4.** Effect of pentoxifylline (POF; 500 mg/4 h) on circulating tumor necrosis factor (TNF) levels in humans after injection of lipopolysaccharide (LPS; 100 ng). TNF levels 2 h after LPS administration were significantly different between treatment with and without POF

Interleukin-6 (IL-6) serum levels showed a significant increase with its maximum 3 h after endo- ... POF treatment did not affect IL-6 levels after endotoxin administration.

... cortisol levels 1 h after endotoxin were much lower than baseline. This fall was followed by an apparent rise with a peak 4 h after endotoxin injection, but the levels had reached the normal range of afternoon cortisol levels 7 h after endotoxin injection. POF treatment did not affect the changes in cortisol levels induced by endotoxin.

... Infusion of POF totally abolished the endotoxin-induced rise in TNF levels. ... This inhibition was selective for TNF without affecting IL-6 levels. ... clinical signs of endotoxemia, such as fever and myalgia as well as high cortisol levels, which are all thought to be provoked by interleukins [13], are not affected by POF treatment.
verdict_explanation: Supported: 10 male volunteers studied on two occasions (within-subject), LPS 100 ng IV bolus (Salmonella abortus equi), infusion started 30 min before and continued 4 h, and statements that IL-6 levels, cortisol changes, and clinical responses/symptoms were not affected by POF. Fig. 4 table supports baseline TNF 20 vs 20 pg/ml and 2 h TNF 38 vs 23 pg/ml, and the figure caption states 2 h levels were significantly different; however, the section provided does not give the specific p-value (p<0.02) for the 2 h TNF difference, and it does not explicitly describe the study as a randomized 'crossover trial' (it says examined on two occasions with saline first and POF second).
readiness_reason: A corrected claim can be faithfully constructed from explicit descriptions and Fig. 4 table/caption: dosing/timing, sample size and responders, TNF baseline and 2 h values, and 'not affected' statements for IL-6, cortisol, and clinical responses. The only needed repair is removing the unsupported p<0.02 and avoiding asserting randomized crossover beyond what is stated.
original_claim: In a crossover trial in healthy male volunteers given 100 ng Salmonella abortus equi LPS IV, pentoxifylline 500 mg IV infused over 4 hours starting 30 minutes before LPS reduced the 2-hour post-LPS serum TNF-α peak from 38 pg/ml to 23 pg/ml (p<0.02), while IL-6 levels, cortisol dynamics, and clinical symptoms (e.g., fever, myalgia, headache, nausea, heart rate, blood pressure) were reported as unaffected by pentoxifylline.

citation.locator: Methods -> Questionnaire and diary; Methods -> Diary and questionnaire on adherence behavior

claim: Alewijnse et al. (2003) assessed PFME adherence using a 7-day diary that measured adherence as the number of days per week women followed the physiotherapist’s behavioral advice; data were collected before treatment (pre-test), immediately after treatment (post-test), and at 3 and 12 months after therapy. The diary adherence item was validated against three questionnaire items, which correlated significantly with the diary item (Spearman r_s = 0.388–0.632, P < 0.001); the questionnaire items asked how often women had adhered the day before, the week before, and asked for a self-evaluation adherence score from 1 to 10.
source_text:
All data were collected with self-administered questionnaires and 7-day diaries before (pre-test), immediately after (post-test), and at 3 and 12 months after therapy. Women received the pre-test survey from the GP's assistants before therapy and the post-test survey from the physiotherapists after the final PFME therapy session. The 3- and 12-month follow-up surveys were mailed to the participants.

... 

The 7-day diary assessed adherence in terms of number of days per week women had followed the physiotherapist's behavioral advice at post-test and follow-ups. To minimize the risk of bias caused by social desirability, a five-point scale was used instead of a dichotomous scale in the diary question on adherence behavior, in which the first three options referred to reasons for non-adher-

ence, the fourth to moderate adherence and the fifth to optimal adherence. Three items on adherence behavior in the questionnaire were used as validation for the diary assessment (Kerssens et al., 1996) that all correlated highly and significantly ( $r_s = 0.388-0.632$ ,  $P < 0.001$ ) with the diary item. These three items assessed how often women had adhered to the behavioral advice the day and the week before, and a self-evaluation score for adherence on a scale from 1 to 10.
verdict_explanation: Supported: adherence operationalization as number of days/week following the physiotherapist's behavioral advice; use of a 7-day diary; measurement times include pre-test, post-test, 3 and 12 months; validation against three questionnaire items with Spearman r_s = 0.388–0.632 and P < 0.001; and the content of the three questionnaire items (day before, week before, and 1–10 self-evaluation). Not supported as written: the claim says the diary was "administered post-treatment, at 3 months, and at 12 months" (the source indicates data were collected also at pre-test, and describes adherence diary assessment at post-test and follow-ups). Also the claim states the diary was "validated" (true) but adds "administered post-treatment" as if only post and later, omitting pre-test measurement, which is a material timing omission. No exact definition phrase "extent" appears; the paper uses operational wording "number of days per week".
readiness_reason: After repair, the claim is directly and specifically supported by verbatim source text, with clear measurement timing and validation statistics/items.
original_claim: Alewijnse et al. (2003) defined PFME adherence as the extent to which participants followed the physiotherapist’s behavioral advice regarding daily home PFME, and quantified it using a validated 7-day diary administered post-treatment, at 3 months, and at 12 months; diary entries were validated against three questionnaire items with Spearman r_s reported as 0.388 to 0.632 (p<0.001).

claim: In chen2004.pdf.md, a 17-item Chen Pelvic Floor Muscle Exercise Self-Efficacy (PFMSE) scale was tested for reliability and validity using data collected from 106 urinary incontinent women recruited from four university-based hospitals in Taiwan (women visiting for PFM rehabilitation from April 6, 2000 to March 31, 2001). Participants’ ages ranged from 24 to 89 years (mean 48.63, SD 11.39). Exploratory factor analysis (principal component analysis with varimax rotation) extracted two factors (eigenvalues 5.81 and 5.53) explaining 34.16% and 32.55% of variance (total 66.71%); Cronbach’s alpha was .92 for Factor I, .94 for Factor II, and .95 for the total scale. source_text: **ABSTRACT:** The purpose of this study was to establish a reliable and valid instrument to evaluate women's confidence in performing pelvic floor muscle exercise (PFME). Data were collected from 106 urinarly incontinent women and the reliability and validity of the scale were tested. The results showed that the scale has a high Cronbach's alpha of .95 for its internal consistency. Test-retest reliability over 6-30 days was $r = .86$ ( $p < .001$ ), showing acceptable stability of the Chen PFMSE scale. Exploratory factor analysis was used to test the initial construct validity, and two factors were extracted, which explained 34.16% and 32.55% of the total variance respectively, with a total of 66.71%. ... ### **Participants** Four university-based hospitals were the data collection sites, two located in central Taiwan, one in northern Taiwan, and the other one in eastern Taiwan. Women visiting one of the four sites for PFM rehabilitation from April 6, 2000 to March 31, 2001 were invited to participate in the study if they met the inclusion criteria. ... Conservative strategies include scheduled voiding, double (or triple) void, or straining to void with manual compression of lower abdomen (Credé maneuver) or abdominal straining (Valsalva maneuver), all of which can be useful to decrease residual urine in UAB patients. The use of indwelling or intermittent urinary catheterization may be instituted in patients who cannot perform the above maneuvers or have started experiencing clinical complications of UAB due to their elevated post-void residual urine. These adverse sequelae may include urinary retention, recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder calculi, and impaired renal function with or without upper renal tract dilatation on radiological imaging.

At present, there is no validated or approved oral therapy in UAB [4], and the current therapy are twofold: (1) decreasing the bladder outlet resistance using  $\alpha$ -adrenergic blockers and (2) promoting bladder contractility with choline esterase inhibitors (e.g., distigmine) [25–27].

source_text: To investigate whether this lower VO2peak is the result of 1) a reduced mitochondrial content, 2) differences in the structure and density of the muscle capillary network and/or 3) an increased imbalance between the protein content and phosphorylation state of eNOS and of the subunits of the NAD(P)H-oxidase protein complex in the muscle microvasculature, muscle biopsies were collected to make these measurements in 7-8 patient/matched control pairs. As the patient/matched control ratio for each of the measured variables was close to 1.0 (Table 4 and Table 5) this leads to the conclusion that the reduction in VO2peak in the patients must be the result of impairments in the blood supply to the exercising muscle or of a reduction in the efficiency of mitochondrial respiration (lower ATP/O ratio) in the exercising muscle.

claim: Gülen (2024) states that confirming a diagnosis of MCAS requires fulfillment of three diagnostic criteria: (1) typical, severe, episodic mast cell activation symptoms in ≥2 organ systems; (2) laboratory evidence of an event-related substantial transient increase in a validated mast cell activation marker during the symptomatic event; and (3) control of symptoms with mast cell mediator–targeting drugs.
source_text:
MCAS may be diagnosed when the symptoms of MC activation are systemic (involving more than one organ system), severe, and recurrent and the MCAS criteria are fulfilled [17••, 18••]. There are three sets of criteria required for an MCAS diagnosis as illustrated in Fig. 1: (1) the presence of typical, severe, episodic MC activation symptoms in  $\geq 2$  organ systems; (2) the detection of a substantial transient increase in a validated marker of MC activation during the symptomatic event; (3) the control of symptoms with MC mediator–targeting drugs.

... 

**Fig. 1** Diagnostic criteria for mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS). All three criteria must be fulfilled to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS: **A** clinical criterion, **B** laboratory criterion; **C** response criterion. Please refer to the text for further explanation

... 

The clinical criterion of MCAS requires the simultaneous involvement of  $\geq 2$  organ systems [17••, 18••].

... 

Secondly, the diagnosis of MCAS requires laboratory proof. Hence, the clinical symptoms of MCAS are associated with an acute, substantial increase in the levels of a validated mediator of systemic MC activation during an episode, either in serum or urine, compared with the patient's baseline levels.

... 

Thirdly, the MCAS diagnosis requires a favorable response to agents that act as MC stabilizers or inhibitors of MC mediators, such as histamine receptor antagonists (H1- and H2-antihistamines), leukotriene blockers, MC stabilizers, and aspirin or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs) [15•, 58, 59•].

readiness_reason: The repaired claim is directly supported by verbatim source language specifying the three criteria and that all three must be fulfilled; no unresolved attributions remain.

citation.locator: TABLE III. Stepwise Multiple Regression for Incontinence at 2nd to 4th Clinic Sessions

claim: In TABLE III of siu2003.pdf.md (Stepwise Multiple Regression for Incontinence at 2nd to 4th Clinic Sessions), the authors report stepwise multiple regression models in which later-visit incontinence episodes are predicted by baseline incontinence episodes and prior-visit compliance and pelvic muscle strength. Specifically: (1) For incontinence episodes at the 3rd clinic (N=171), predictors include baseline incontinence episodes (β=0.72, P<0.001), compliance at 2nd clinic (β=-0.19, P<0.001), and pelvic muscle strength at 2nd clinic (β=-0.16, P=0.001), with R²=0.64 and F=100.64 (table footnote indicates *P<0.001 for F). (2) For incontinence episodes at the 4th clinic (N=111), predictors include baseline incontinence episodes (β=0.50, P<0.001), compliance at 3rd clinic (β=-0.38, P<0.001), and pelvic muscle strength at 3rd clinic (β=-0.16, P<0.05), with R²=0.52 and F=37.32 (table footnote indicates *P<0.001 for F).
source_text:
**TABLE III. Stepwise Multiple Regression for Incontinence at 2nd to 4th Clinic Sessions**

|                                                 | N   | $\beta$ | P      | R<sup>2</sup> | F       |
|-------------------------------------------------|-----|---------|--------|---------------|---------|
| Incontinence episodes at 3<sup>rd</sup> clinic  |     |         |        |               |         |
| Baseline incontinence episodes                  | 171 | 0.72    | <0.001 | 0.64          | 100.64* |
| Compliance at 2<sup>nd</sup> clinic             |     | -0.19   | <0.001 |               |         |
| Pelvic muscle strength at 2<sup>nd</sup> clinic |     | -0.16   | 0.001  |               |         |
| Incontinence episodes at 4<sup>th</sup> clinic  |     |         |        |               |         |
| Baseline incontinence episodes                  | 111 | 0.50    | <0.001 | 0.52          | 37.32*  |
| Compliance at 3<sup>rd</sup> clinic             |     | -0.38   | <0.001 |               |         |
| Pelvic muscle strength at 3<sup>rd</sup> clinic |     | -0.16   | <0.05  |               |         |

\* $P < 0.001$ .

claim: Human PMNs incubated 30 min at 37°C with pentoxifylline 300 µg/ml had reduced adherence to nylon vs diluent control: 64.1 ± 2.7% (n=16) in diluent vs 54.0 ± 3.9% (n=6; P=0.031) with pentoxifylline.
source_text: There was  $64.1 \pm 2.7\%$  ( $n = 16$ ) PMN adherence to nylon when PMNs were incubated for 30 min at 37°C in diluent. Incubation of the PMNs for 30 min with pentoxifylline (300  $\mu\text{g/ml}$ ) decreased PMN adherence to  $54.0 \pm 3.9\%$  ( $n = 6$ ;  $P = 0.031$ ).
verdict_explanation: Adherence: baseline 64.1±2.7% (n=16) vs PTX 300 µg/ml 54.0±3.9% (n=6; P=0.031) is exactly supported; IL-1 (100 U/ml) adherence 79.6±3.2% (n=11; P=0.001) and PTX 300 µg/ml lowering to 60.4±4.1% (n=6; P=0.002) is exactly supported. Migration: IL-1 (150 U/ml) decreases directed migration to 1.57±0.12 mm and PTX 100 µg/ml restores to 2.39±0.11 mm with (n=3; P<0.005) is exactly supported; the candidate’s attribution 'improved/“restored” directed migration inhibited by LPS-MCM/TNF/IL-1' is directionally consistent with the section, but the candidate highlights only IL-1 and does not supply the LPS-MCM/TNF numeric pairs (the paper does provide some LPS-MCM and PTX numbers in text, but the candidate’s specific IL-1 example is supported). Superoxide: the FMLP-stimulated reduction 1.68±0.37 to 0.67±0.11 nmol/10 min/10^6 PMNs at PTX 100 µg/ml (n=5; P=0.038) is exactly supported. Degranulation: the paper reports that PTX (1 and 100 µg/ml) decreased lysozyme release from LPS-MCM-treated PMNs with only 'P < 0.050' and refers to Fig. 8; it does not provide the specific numeric lysozyme values for the PTX conditions in the running text, so the candidate’s generic '(P<0.050)' is only partially verifiable as stated and lacks the specific values/conditions beyond what the text provides. Calcium: FMLP 1 nM raises [Ca2+]i to 115.07±18.96 nM and PTX 300 µg/ml lowers to 33.11±11.90 nM (n=5; P=0.025) is exactly supported. FMLP binding: at 37°C PTX 1 mM increases specific [3H]FMLP binding from 5.73×10^3±0.95×10^3 to 7.74×10^3±0.68×10^3 molecules/PMN (P=0.002) is exactly supported; note the paper specifies 1 mM = 278 µg/ml. Also, the candidate mentions PTX '100–300 µg/ml' generally; 100 and 300 µg/ml are indeed used across assays, but the specific adherence baseline comparison is at 300 µg/ml.
readiness_reason: Fully supported with exact values, n, incubation time/temp, and P-value.

claim: In 12 pigs (25–35 kg) given fecal peritonitis induced by intraperitoneal spread of 35 mL aspirated cecal content, six animals received a pentoxifylline (PTF) infusion of 60 mg/h started 120 minutes before peritonitis induction and maintained for the study duration; animals were killed 300 minutes after peritonitis induction. In hemodynamic results, the peritonitis (test/untreated) group had SVR increase to 133% above baseline at 300 minutes versus 36% above baseline in the PTF group at 300 minutes, with significant differences between groups at all points from baseline to 300 minutes except at 30 minutes; PVR reached 462% above baseline (test) versus 140% above baseline (PTF) at 300 minutes, with significant between-group differences at 270 and 300 minutes; MAP decreased to 65% of baseline (test) and 71% of baseline (PTF) at 300 minutes, with a significant difference between groups at 180 and 210 minutes.
source_text:
Anesthesia was induced in 12 pigs (25 to 35 kg) with azaperone (2.0 mg/kg im) and metomidate (10 mg/kg ip). ... A laparotomy was performed and 35 ml of aspirated cecal content was spread in the peritoneum to induce peritonitis (PI). In six animals an infusion of PTF (60 mg/h) was started 120 min before PI and maintained for the study duration. ... The animals were killed 300 min after PI.

In the test group, MAP decreased progressively to 65% of baseline at 300 min (Fig. 1). The baseline value was not significantly lower in the PTF group and after PI there was a similar pattern with MAP decreasing to 71% of baseline at 300 min. There was a significant difference between the two groups at 180 and 210 min.

In the test group there was a progressive increase in SVR to 133% above baseline at 300 min. In marked contrast, SVR increased only to 36% above baseline in the PTF group at 300 min. There were significant differences between the two groups at all points from baseline to 300 min other than at 30 min.

In both groups, PVR increased progressively, reaching a maximum 462% above baseline in the test group and 140% above baseline in the PTF group at 300 min. There were significant differences between the two groups at 270 and 300 min.
verdict_explanation: Supported: species/weight range; fecal peritonitis induction method and volume; PTF infusion rate (60 mg/h), start time (120 min before PI), and maintained for study duration; animals killed 300 min after PI; SVR and PVR percent-above-baseline values at 300 min and which time points showed significant between-group differences; MAP percent-of-baseline at 300 min and significant between-group differences at 180 and 210 min. Not supported as written: (1) the claim that MAP was "higher" in the PTF-pretreated group at 180 and 210 min (the source states only that there was a significant difference, and also reports overall similar MAP pattern with no significant differences in MAP in the abstract/summary statement: "No significant differences were seen in MAP..."); (2) explicit p-values of p<0.05 for those specific MAP/SVR/PVR time points are not stated in the Hemodynamics text (significance is described without giving exact p-values); (3) the observation period is described as animals killed 300 min after PI, but the source does not explicitly phrase this as a "300-minute post-induction observation period"; (4) "untreated peritonitis pigs" group size is not explicitly stated in the methods text (it states 12 pigs total and 6 with PTF; the remaining peritonitis test group size is inferable but not explicitly stated). Provisional label corrected from PRECLINICAL (already appropriate) and maintained.
readiness_reason: After repair, the claim is directly supported by explicit methods and hemodynamics text with no unresolved attributions; removed/avoided unsupported directions about MAP being higher and exact p-values, and avoided unstated group size for the untreated peritonitis group.
original_claim: In domestic pigs (25–35 kg) with fecal peritonitis, pentoxifylline was infused IV continuously at 60 mg/h starting 120 minutes before peritonitis induction and continued through a 300-minute post-induction observation period; compared with untreated peritonitis pigs, the PTX-pretreated group had higher MAP at 180 and 210 minutes (p<0.05), lower SVR increases at 300 minutes (+36% vs +133% above baseline; p<0.05 at all time points except 30 min), and lower PVR increases at 300 minutes (+140% vs +462% above baseline; significant at 270 and 300 min, p<0.05).

claim: In this pig fecal peritonitis study, neutrophil adhesiveness was measured by circulating 35 mL of whole blood in a 37°C chamber containing glass cover slips; neutrophil counts were taken over time and the time for the neutrophil count to decline to 50% of baseline was calculated as the half clearance time (with decreased adhesiveness expressed as increased half clearance time).
source_text: Thirty-five milliliters of blood was circulated in a temperature-controlled chamber at 37°C containing glass cover slips to which the neutrophils adhered. Neutrophil counts were made on samples taken from the chamber at 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 min. The time for the neutrophil count to decline to 50% of the baseline value was calculated and expressed as the half clearance time. A decrease in neutrophil adhesiveness is thus expressed as an increase in the half clearance time.

readiness_reason: Directly supported procedural description with exact definition of half clearance time.
original_claim: In the swine fecal peritonitis model, neutrophil adhesiveness measured by in vitro glass cover-slip clearance half-time was reportedly unchanged in untreated peritonitis pigs, while PTX pretreatment increased half-clearance time by 100% before peritonitis induction and by a further 238% at 30 minutes post-induction (p<0.05 vs baseline; p<0.05 vs untreated at both time points); TEM at 5 hours reportedly showed severe lung/liver/spleen microvascular leukostasis and tissue injury in untreated peritonitis that was largely prevented in PTX-pretreated pigs (maintained capillary/sinusoidal patency, reduced endothelial injury, prevented neutrophil degranulation).

claim: Vogel et al. describe a monocentric, retrospective observational study conducted in Munich using longitudinal data from 80 patients with Cushing’s syndrome who were prospectively enrolled in the German Cushing’s Registry between 2012 and 2021; patients were studied during active CS at diagnosis immediately before surgery and during postoperative remission follow-up visits at 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 months after surgery.
source_text:
Abstract

**Setting:** In this retrospective observational study, we analyzed longitudinal data from 80 patients with CS prospectively enrolled in the German Cushing's registry between 2012 and 2021. ... The patients were studied during active CS and in the postoperative remission phase 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 months after surgery.

...

## Methods

### Patients

This monocentric, retrospective observational study of patients with endogenous CS was carried out between 2012 and 2021 in Munich as part of the German Cushing's Registry (NeoExNet, No. 152-10). ...

In a first step, 80 patients were included and studied at the time of diagnosis immediately before surgery and thereafter following curative surgery. ... Postoperative clinical and biochemical control examinations were conducted at 1, 3, 6, 12, and

24 months, respectively.
verdict_explanation: Supported: monocentric, retrospective observational design; longitudinal data; 80 patients; prospectively enrolled in the German Cushing’s registry; 2012–2021; studied at diagnosis immediately before surgery (active CS) and followed at 1/3/6/12/24 months after surgery. Not fully supported as written: the claim adds "adult" and "overt endogenous" and "in surgical remission"—the Methods specify "overt endogenous CS" but do not explicitly state "adult". The claim also specifies "LMU Munich" in the registry description; the source states the study was carried out "in Munich" and gives the authors’ affiliation (LMU Munich), but the registry itself is not explicitly labeled "LMU Munich" in the cited passages. Table 1 does not list these follow-up timepoints (it summarizes baseline and 6-month remission characteristics only).
readiness_reason: The repaired claim is directly and specifically supported by verbatim text in the Abstract and Methods > Patients, including design, registry enrollment timing, sample size, and follow-up schedule. Any unsupported qualifiers from the original candidate (e.g., 'adult' and Table 1 covering all timepoints) have been removed or corrected.

(2023) report a monocentric, retrospective observational study using prospectively collected data from the German Cushing's Registry (LMU Munich, 2012–2021), including 80 adult patients with overt endogenous Cushing’s syndrome in surgical remission who were assessed at baseline (active CS pre-op) and at 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 months after curative surgery.

claim: In Vogel et al. (2023), inflammatory status was evaluated using CRP and IL-6 (and, in a 25-patient subgroup with matched controls, also total IgG). CRP increased from median 0.10 mg dL−1 (IQR 0.06–0.39) during active CS (n=80) to median 0.48 mg dL−1 (IQR 0.14–0.90) at 1 month after surgery (n=66; P≤.001 vs active CS). In the 25-patient subgroup, IL-6 increased from median 1.7 pg mL−1 (IQR 1.5–2.5) during active CS to median 7.2 pg mL−1 (IQR 3.3–11.7) at 1 month after surgery (P≤.001 vs active CS) and was higher than matched controls (median 2.0 pg mL−1 [1.5–3.6], P≤.001). In a post-hoc analysis dividing the 25-patient subgroup by BMI at the time of active CS, patients with BMI >30 kg m−2 had higher 1-month IL-6 (median 9.2 pg mL−1 [6.1–13.7]) than those with BMI <30 kg m−2 (median 4.0 pg mL−1 [2.5–9.1], P=.03).
source_text:
### Laboratory analyses

Venous blood samples were drawn following overnight fasting at the time of diagnosis and as part of the follow-up visits after successful surgery. The biochemical analyses were performed in the laboratory of the Endocrine Department and in the Institute of Laboratory Medicine of Ludwig-Maximilians-University Hospital Munich using standard methods. Measurements of interleukin-6 (IL-6), C-reactive protein (CRP) and total immunoglobulin G (IgG) of the subgroup of 25 patients with CS and 25 age-, gender-, and BMI-matched control subjects were made in one run at the end of the observation period using a Cobas 8000 analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany).
...
### Remission phase after surgery for CS is characterized by a state of low-grade inflammation

In the cohort of 80 patients, early remission 1 month after surgery was characterized by a 4.8-fold increase in CRP concentrations compared with the time of active CS [median CRP 0.48 mg dL<sup>-1</sup> (0.14–0.90) vs 0.10 mg dL<sup>-1</sup> (0.06–0.39),  $P \leq .001$ ].
...
**Figure 1.** C-reactive protein (mg dL<sup>-1</sup>; reference ≤0.5 mg dL<sup>-1</sup>, dashed line) during active Cushing's syndrome (CS) and after successful operation (OP) up to 24 months (mo). Active CS *n* = 80, 1 mo *n* = 66, 3 mo *n* = 61, 6 mo *n* = 75, 12 mo *n* = 73, 24 mo *n* = 65.
...
Interleukin-6 levels showed a 4.2-fold increase 1 month after surgery compared with the time point of active CS [median IL-6 7.2 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (3.3–11.7) vs 1.7 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (1.5–2.5),  $P \leq .001$ ], and an elevation of more than 3-fold compared with the 25 matched control subjects [median IL-6 7.2 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (3.3–11.7) vs 2.0 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (1.5–3.6),  $P \leq .001$ ].
...
When dividing the patient subgroup in a post-hoc analysis according to BMI < 30 kg m<sup>-2</sup> and BMI > 30 kg m<sup>-2</sup> at the time of active CS, inflammatory markers revealed significant differences between the groups (Figure 3), with a median IL-6 of 9.2 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (6.1–13.7) in BMI > 30 kg m<sup>-2</sup> at 1 month follow-up compared with 4.0 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (2.5–9.1) in BMI < 30 kg m<sup>-2</sup> ( $P = .03$ ; Figure 3A).
verdict_explanation: All numeric CRP and IL-6 values, n's, and P-values are supported at the cited locations, and the BMI stratification is explicitly defined as BMI at the time of active CS. citation.locator: Discussion; Discussion > Limitations, strengths, and outlook; Conclusion

claim: In this retrospective observational study of postoperative remission in Cushing’s syndrome, Vogel et al. (2023) report that CRP and IL-6 during early remission correlated inversely with muscle function during follow-up, and state that CRP and IL-6 could serve as easily measurable biomarkers/surrogate parameters for clinical features of glucocorticoid withdrawal syndrome (with potential use for monitoring glucocorticoid replacement adjustments), while emphasizing that the observational design demonstrates associations, not causation, and noting it is unclear whether the inflammation–myopathy relationship is associative or causal.
source_text:
Thus, our study provides evidence that easily measurable quantitative biomarkers—CRP and IL-6—could serve as surrogate parameters for the clinical features of glucocorticoid withdrawal syndrome and could potentially be used to monitor adjustments of the glucocorticoid replacement dose. However, this has yet to be shown in a prospective study with specific assessment of glucocorticoid

withdrawal syndrome. ... Nevertheless, it is unclear whether this is an association or causally related given that the molecular processes underlying glucocorticoid-induced myopathy are poorly understood.

...

This is an observational study and therefore demonstrates only associations and not causation.

...

C-reactive protein and IL-6 could serve as biomarkers to monitor patients during the glucocorticoid withdrawal phase.
verdict_explanation: Supported that the authors describe CRP/IL-6 as potential surrogate parameters/biomarkers to monitor glucocorticoid withdrawal phase and report inverse correlations with muscle function during follow-up, including 12 months (1 year) outcomes. The limitation language is explicitly stated by the authors (“observational… only associations and not causation”), and the Discussion explicitly says it is unclear whether the relationship is association vs causal. However, the candidate over-specifies timing and directionality as “early post-operative CRP and IL-6 elevations” being “predictive biomarkers” for “prolonged glucocorticoid withdrawal symptoms” and “delayed functional muscle recovery”: the paper frames these as correlations/associations and potential surrogate parameters/biomarkers; it does not explicitly claim prediction, does not explicitly state “prolonged symptoms,” and does not present CRP/IL-6 as validated surrogate endpoints. Also, the muscle-function association is described for CRP and IL-6 together in univariate analysis; multivariable significance is stated specifically for CRP (3 months) and muscle function (1 year).
readiness_reason: Key elements (biomarker/surrogate language; association with muscle function; non-causation limitation; unclear association vs causality statement) are directly supported by quoted source text with clear locators and can be faithfully compressed without adding prediction/validation claims.

source_text: *Administration of PTX.* One hour after CLP, animals were re-anesthetized with methoxyflurane inhalation and the femoral vein was cannulated using PE-50 tubing. PTX (50 mg/kg body wt in 1 mL normal saline solution; Sigma, St. Louis, MO) was infused through the venous catheter at a constant infusion rate over a period of 90 min. ... Vehicle-treated septic animals received 1 mL normal saline solution intravenously for 90 min. Sham-operated animals received neither PTX nor saline.

citation.locator: MATERIALS AND METHODS; Intracellular and Extracellular Water and Electrolyte Partition

claim: Intracellular and extracellular water/electrolyte partition was calculated using chloride space as extracellular fluid estimate and assuming passive chloride distribution related to measured resting membrane potential as predicted by the Nernst equation; intracellular chloride was calculated using the Nernst equation, and intracellular sodium and potassium concentrations were computed from total muscle ion content and water partitioning.
source_text:
At each time point, the intracellular distribution of electrolytes and water was calculated from the striated muscle cell membrane potential, total water, and the plasma and muscle concentration of sodium, potassium, and chloride by applying the Nernst equation.

### *Intracellular and Extracellular Water and Electrolyte Partition*

The partition of water and electrolytes between the intracellular and extracellular phases was calculated on the basis of the chloride space as the estimate of extracellular fluid volume. Intracellular and extracellular chloride distribution was considered to be a passive phenomenon, related to the measured resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle in a manner predicted by the Nernst equation.

Intracellular chloride was calculated as follows:

$$\text{PD} = -61.5 \log \frac{\text{CLo}}{\text{CLi}} \quad \text{CLi} = \frac{\text{CLo}}{\text{antilog } \text{PD}/-61.5}$$

... allows computation of the [Nai] and [Ki] intracellular concentrations, as follows:

$$[\text{Nai}] = \frac{\text{Nats} - (\text{ECW} \times [\text{Nao}])}{\text{ICW}} \quad [\text{Ki}] = \frac{\text{Kts} - (\text{ECW} \times [\text{Ko}])}{\text{ICW}}$$

source_text:
Table 1 shows the results of the preoperative adrenal-function tests in these 3 patients and the other 21 patients. All had elevated plasma cortisol concentrations, which varied little during the day, increased urinary 17-hydroxycorticosteroid excretion, and normal urinary 17-ketosteroid excretion. The administration of dexamethasone did not reduce either the plasma cortisol concentration or the urinary excretion of 17-hydroxycorticosteroid in any patient. No differences were noted in these respects between the 3 patients in whom thyroid dysfunction later developed and the other 21 patients.

Among these 24 patients with Cushing's syndrome due to a hyperfunctioning adrenocortical adenoma, 5 patients, including the 3 in whom thyroid dysfunction subsequently developed, had increased antimicrosomal-antibody titers.

Of the remaining 21 patients with a hyperfunctioning adrenocortical adenoma, 2 had positive antimicrosomal-antibody titers (1:100 in both) and negative antithyroglobulin-antibody titers at first. After surgery, the antimicrosomal-antibody titers for these patients did not change, and their thyroid function remained normal. The remaining 19 patients had no symptoms or signs of thyroid disease, no abnormalities in thyroid-function tests, and no thyroid autoantibodies at any time after the operation.

source_text:
***Patients and Methods:* Twenty-four eligible women with 29 RIF areas involving the skin and underlying tissues were enrolled from December 1998 to April 2000. These patients, previously irradiated for breast cancer, were randomly assigned to four balanced treatment groups: (A) 800 mg/d of PTX and 1,000 U/d of Vit E; (B) PTX plus placebo; (C) placebo plus Vit E; and (D) placebo-placebo. The main end point measure was the relative regression of measurable RIF surface after 6 months of treatment.

***Results:* Twenty-two patients with 27 RIF areas were analyzed at 6 months. Mean RIF surface regression was significant with combined PTX/Vit E versus double placebo (60% ± 10% *v* 43% ± 17%; *P* = .038).

To assess the efficacy and synergism of PTX and Vit E as an antifibrotic treatment in patients with measurable areas of symptomatic chronic radiotherapy damage, we performed the present monocentric, double-blind, randomized clinical trial of combined PTX/Vit E versus placebo. A  $2 \times 2$  factorial design was used to allow testing for drug interactions and the marginal effects of each treatment.

In an individual double-blind design, the 24 women included were randomly assigned, for 6 months, to a combination of 800 mg/d of PTX in two 400-mg tablets and 1,000 U/d of Vit E in two 500-U capsules (group A), PTX and placebo capsules (group B), placebo tablets and Vit E (group C), and placebo tablets and capsules (group D).

For the main treatment comparison (A *v* D) involving the main and secondary end points, we used the Wilcoxon rank sum test.

At 6 months, we observed a significant mean RIF surface regression of 60% with combined PTX/Vit E in group A, versus 43% for double placebo in group D ( $P = .038$ ).

Design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
