“Design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.”

“Setting: Surgical intensive care units at 2 university hospitals.”

“Patients: Fifty-one surgical patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline continuously (27 patients) or saline infusion as placebo (24 patients).”

“Interventions: Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.”
verdict_explanation: Randomization/blinding/placebo control, setting (surgical ICUs), N and group sizes, dose (1 mg/kg/h continuous infusion), lack of between-group differences in TNF-α and IL-6 bioactivity “during the study,” MOD score significance on day 14 with “Student t test with Bonferroni correction,” PaO2/FiO2 significance on days 14 and 17 (with Bonferroni wording in the figure caption), and mortality denominators with log-rank P values (0.85; 0.43) are supported. However, the candidate over-specifies organ-function results for PAHR as “lower from Day 6 through Day 28, p < 0.05”; the source states significance on day 6 and that it “remained decreased,” but does not state that PAHR was statistically significantly lower for every timepoint from day 6 through day 28.
readiness_reason: Directly quoted study design, setting, sample size/allocation, and dosing.
original_claim: In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial in surgical ICU severe sepsis (N=51; PTX 27 vs placebo 24), pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg/h continuous infusion) showed no statistically significant differences vs placebo in systemic TNF-α bioactivity or IL-6 bioactivity over 28 days, yet was reported to improve organ-function measures (Marshall MOD score reduced on Day 14, p < 0.05 with Bonferroni correction; PaO2/FiO2 improved on Days 14 and 17, p < 0.05; PAHR lower from Day 6 through Day 28, p < 0.05). ***Summary*** Oxpentifylline (pentoxifylline) ... was tested in human beings after injection of endotoxin. ... ## Results
... Eight of the remaining nine subjects responded to endotoxin with symptoms such as myalgia and headache ... Two subjects also had nausea ... Systolic and diastolic blood pressure were not affected. None of the clinical responses to endotoxin were affected by oxpentifylline.

... In contrast, during oxpentifylline treatment there was no rise in serum TNF (baseline: 23 [7] pg/ml, 2 h after endotoxin 24 [5] pg/ml). The difference in TNF levels 2 h after endotoxin between the saline infusion and oxpentifylline infusion periods was significant (p < 0·02).

... Oxpentifylline treatment did not affect IL-6 serum levels after endotoxin administration (fig 2).

... Oxpentifylline treatment did not affect the changes in cortisol levels provoked by endotoxin (fig 3).

## Discussion
Infusion of oxpentifylline totally abolished the endotoxin-induced rise in TNF. ... We found that treatment with oxpentifylline caused selective inhibition of TNF without affecting IL-6 levels. ... clinical signs of endotoxaemia, such as fever and myalgia as well as high cortisol levels, ... are not affected by oxpentifylline treatment.
verdict_explanation: Part (a) about the endotoxaemia volunteer study is supported by the provided Zabel et al text: oxpentifylline abolished the endotoxin-induced rise in serum TNF, while clinical symptoms/fever and cortisol and IL-6 responses were not affected. readiness_reason: Single-source, directly stated findings with exact supporting quotations available in the provided text.

source_text: Poyhonen et al. [1] reported the natural course of male LUTS without treatment in a population-based cohort study. readiness_reason: This child claim matches the review’s wording, definitions, time horizon, and age-at-baseline, and does not introduce unstated percentages or treatment-type qualifiers.

claim: In a narrative review on medical therapies for BPH/LUTS in older men, the authors state that common side effects of alpha-blockers include dizziness and orthostatic hypotension; they further state that in older adults these effects are major concerns because they can lead to falls and subsequent injuries. The review also reports that the FORTA classification labels silodosin and tamsulosin as “caution” due to risks of hypotension, especially with other anti-hypertensive medications, and labels alfuzosin, doxazosin, and terazosin as “avoid” due to increased risk for orthostatic hypotension and syncope (among other listed risks).
source_text: The most common side effects of alpha-blockers include dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, retrograde ejaculation, and rhinitis. In older adults, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension are major concerns as they can lead to falls and subsequent injuries. ... The FORTA classification system for medications in older adults studied the various alpha-blockers commercially available and labeled silodosin and tamsulosin as “caution” due to there being no data on efficacy and safety in older people and for their risks of hypotension, especially in the setting of other anti-hypertensive medications. It labeled alfuzosin, doxazosin, and terazosin as “avoid” due to their increased risk for orthostatic hypotension, vasodilatory effects, cardiac arrhythmias, and syncope [15••].
verdict_explanation: Supported that the narrative review links alpha-blockers to dizziness and orthostatic hypotension and explicitly states these can lead to falls/injuries in older adults. Supported that it reports FORTA ratings: silodosin/tamsulosin = “caution” due to hypotension risk especially with other anti-hypertensives; alfuzosin/doxazosin/terazosin = “avoid” due to increased orthostatic hypotension and syncope risk (and other risks). However, the candidate additionally claims the review states that “combining alpha-blockers with antihypertensives increases additive orthostatic hypotension/syncope risk.” The provided text supports hypotension risk “especially in the setting of other anti-hypertensive medications,” but does not explicitly state additive risk or explicitly mention syncope risk specifically from the combination (syncope is listed as a reason for ‘avoid’ for certain agents, not explicitly as a combination effect). Evidence label should not be primary [CLINICAL] trial evidence; this is a narrative review summarizing other literature.
readiness_reason: After removing/avoiding the unsupported “additive” interaction wording, the remaining claim is directly supported by explicit sentences in the specified section, including the dizziness/orthostatic hypotension → falls/injuries statement and the FORTA “caution” vs “avoid” classifications with reasons.
original_claim: A narrative review of BPH/LUTS medical therapies in older men reports that alpha-blockers are associated with dizziness and orthostatic hypotension (with falls/injuries) and states that combining alpha-blockers with antihypertensives increases additive orthostatic hypotension/syncope risk; it further reports that under the FORTA scale, non-selective alpha-blockers are classified as 'Avoid' and selective agents (tamsulosin/silodosin) as 'Caution' due to hypotensive risks with concurrent antihypertensives.

source_text:
#### 7.3.11. Botulinum toxin

Botulinum toxin is a powerful site-specific muscle relaxant. Botulinum toxin A (BTX-A) has been widely used in treatment of neurogenic bladder and showed efficacy in reduction of bladder outlet resistance and residual urine volume [116,117]. It is a promising alternative for treating refractory sphincter spasticity. It can decrease the need for lifelong CIC [116]. Injection of BTX-A into the urethral sphincter can relax the sphincter and thus reduce bladder outlet resistance and improve bladder emptying in UAB patients [6]. In a study by Liao and Kuo, a success rate of 97% was reported after urethral injections of BTX-A in 32 patients with idiopathic UAB. Also, a success rate of 76% was obtained in 33 patients with detrusor areflexia [118].
verdict_explanation: Supported: The source states that Liao and Kuo reported a 97% success rate in 32 patients with idiopathic UAB and a 76% success rate in 33 patients with detrusor areflexia after urethral injections of BTX-A. Not supported in this source: (1) the explicit numerators/denominators "31/32" and "25/33" are not given here; only percentages and denominators (32; 33) appear. (2) the injection target is stated only as "urethral sphincter"; the specific phrasing "striated external sphincter" is not present in the named source text.
readiness_reason: A repaired claim limited to what the review explicitly reports (percent success and denominators; urethral sphincter injections; populations) is directly supported by verbatim source text at the stated location; unsupported specifics (numerators and "striated external sphincter") were removed.

claim: In Staubach et al. (1998), 51 surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline by continuous intravenous infusion at 1 mg/kg body weight per hour (maximum 1800 mg/day) for 28 days or until discharge from the ICU or death; pentoxifylline concentrations were measured by gas-liquid chromatography; the median serum pentoxifylline concentration was 3628 ng/mL on day 1 and 1620 ng/mL on day 2 and reached a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study; the first metabolite (BL 194) showed a similar pattern and had 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher serum concentrations than the parent drug.
source_text:
**Interventions:** Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.

Fifty-one surgical patients were randomly assigned within 12 hours after diagnosis of sepsis to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (Rentyllin, Rentschler, Germany) 1 mg/kg of body weight per hour, to a maximum of 1800 mg/d or normal saline solution as placebo during 28 days or until patients were discharged from the ICU or died.

Pentoxifylline concentrations were measured by gas-liquid chromatography described by Bryce and Burrows<sup>27</sup> with a detection limit of 3 ng/mL.

The median serum concentration of pentoxifylline was 3628 ng/mL on the first day after starting infusion and 1620 ng/mL on day 2; it reached a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study. A similar pattern was demonstrated for the first metabolite of pentoxifylline (BL 194) with a 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher serum concentration than the parent drug (**Figure 5**).

claim: Kaplan et al. (1997) state that pseudodyssynergia was diagnosed using criteria including: (1) electrical activity of the external sphincter during voiding in the absence of abdominal straining; (2) brief, intermittent closing of the membranous urethra during voiding detected on electromyography and fluoroscopy; and (3) uroflowmetry in a private setting showing an undulating flow pattern, performed to minimize false-positive findings due to performance anxiety (“bashful voiding”) during urodynamic evaluation.
source_text:
**Materials and Methods:** The video urodynamic studies of 43 men 23 to 50 years old with chronic voiding dysfunction secondary to pseudodyssynergia performed between January 1990 and June 1996 were retrospectively analyzed. Pseudodyssynergia was diagnosed based on several criteria, including electrical activity of the external sphincter during voiding in the absence of abdominal straining, and brief and intermittent closing of the membranous urethra during voiding detected by electromyography and fluoroscopy. ...

Pseudodyssynergia was diagnosed based on several criteria, including electrical activity of the external sphincter during voiding in the absence of abdominal straining and brief, intermittent closing of the membranous urethra during voiding detected on electromyography and fluoroscopy (figs. 1

and 2). In addition, to diagnose pseudodyssynergia patients also had to undergo uroflowmetry measurement in a private setting showing intermittent increases and decreases of flow in an undulating fashion. This study was done in an effort to minimize the potential for false-positive results in the face of performance anxiety or “bashful voiding” during the urodynamic evaluation.
verdict_explanation: The source explicitly supports the diagnostic criteria: external sphincter electrical activity during voiding without abdominal straining; brief/intermittent closing of the membranous urethra during voiding detected on EMG and fluoroscopy; and private-setting uroflowmetry to minimize false-positives from performance anxiety (“bashful voiding”). However, the candidate adds details not stated in the checked sections: it specifies "synchronous video pressure-flow with EMG" as part of the diagnostic triad (the paper mentions "video urodynamic studies" and that patients underwent "synchronous video pressure-flow urodynamic evaluation," but the quoted diagnostic criteria do not explicitly say the diagnostic requirement is a *synchronous video pressure-flow with EMG*), it adds "fluoroscopic evidence of intermittent closure/cutoff at the membranous urethral sphincter" (the text supports intermittent closing of the membranous urethra detected on EMG and fluoroscopy; "cutoff" phrasing appears in a figure caption outside the requested abstract/methods triad wording), and it adds "uncatheterized" and "private-room" plus "artifact from examiner presence" (the text says "private setting" but does not specify uncatheterized or examiner presence as the mechanism).
readiness_reason: A repaired, source-faithful claim is fully supported in the ABSTRACT (Materials and Methods) and MATERIALS AND METHODS, with exact quotations for each diagnostic element and the rationale for private-setting uroflowmetry.
original_claim: Kaplan et al. (1997) describe a diagnostic approach for pseudodyssynergia using synchronous video pressure-flow with EMG showing increased external sphincter activity during voiding (without abdominal straining) plus fluoroscopic evidence of intermittent closure/cutoff at the membranous urethral sphincter, and they require uncatheterized private-room uroflowmetry to exclude performance-anxiety ("bashful voiding") artifacts from examiner presence.

claim: In a pilot experiment in male rats (n=6), 45 minutes before induction of hemorrhage, rats received an intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (PTX) 40 mg/kg over 15 minutes. During PTX infusion, mean arterial pressure decreased (112 ± 2.0 to 84.4 ± 14.0 mmHg; p<0.05) and heart rate increased (365 ± 79 to 437 ± 38 beats/min; p<0.05). Total circulating leukocytes increased (7,140 ± 1,460 to 12,700 ± 2,980 cells/mm3; p<0.05), circulating PMNs increased (1,825 ± 280 to 4,055 ± 225 cells/mm3; p<0.05), and the absolute number of circulating NBT-positive PMNs increased (220 ± 218 to 609 ± 635 cells/mm3; p<0.05). When rats with such high NBT-positive PMN counts were subjected to the shock protocol, they all died.
source_text: 1) In this set of pilot experiments (n = 6), 45 minutes before the induction of hemorrhage the rats received an intravenous infusion of 40 mg/kg of PTX over a period of 15 minutes. During the PTX infusion, the animals showed a decrease in mean arterial pressure (MAP); from  $112 \pm 2.0$  mmHg to  $84.4 \pm 14.0$  mmHg ( $p < 0.05$ ). Throughout this period the heart rate was increased from  $365 \pm 79$  beats/min to  $437 \pm 38$  beats/min ( $p < 0.05$ ). The total number of circulating leukocytes was increased in all rats after this mode of PTX administration; from  $7,140 \pm 1,460$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> before infusion to  $12,700 \pm 2,980$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> at 45 minutes after infusion ( $p < 0.05$ ). The number of circulating PMNs was also increased with an average of  $1,825 \pm 280$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> before the PTX infusion to  $4,055 \pm 225$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> at 45 minutes after PTX infusion ( $p < 0.05$ ). This was not associated with a significant increase in the percent of circulating NBT-positive PMNs; from  $12.0 \pm 9.7\%$  to  $15.0 \pm 12.3\%$ . As a consequence, the absolute number of circulating NBT-positive PMNs appeared was higher after the acute PTX treatment, on average to  $609 \pm 635$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> compared with  $220 \pm 218$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> before the PTX infusion ( $p < 0.05$ ). When rats with such high NBT-positive PMN count were subjected to the current shock protocol, they all died.
verdict_explanation: The source supports the species/sex (male rats), acute IV infusion dose (40 mg/kg over 15 minutes) given 45 minutes before induction of hemorrhage, n=6, and the reported MAP/HR/WBC/PMN/absolute NBT(+) PMN values with p<0.05. However, the candidate claim adds details not stated in the source: it labels the post-infusion changes explicitly as "hypotension, tachycardia, leukocytosis, neutrophilia" (interpretive but consistent), and it states "100% mortality (0/6 survival)" after hemorrhagic shock; the source only states, without providing a denominator at the shock stage, "they all died" when subjected to the shock protocol. Also, the source notes there was not a significant increase in the *percent* NBT-positive PMNs (12.0±9.7% to 15.0±12.3%), which the candidate omits; the candidate focuses on the absolute NBT(+) count increase, which is supported.
readiness_reason: A repaired claim can be faithfully constructed from the quoted passage, with mortality phrased as "they all died" rather than asserting an explicit 0/6 denominator.
original_claim: In male rats, an acute PTX IV regimen (40 mg/kg over 15 minutes) given 45 minutes prior to hemorrhage caused significant hypotension (MAP 112±2.0 to 84.4±14.0 mmHg, P<0.05), tachycardia (HR 365±79 to 437±38 bpm, P<0.05), leukocytosis (WBC 7,140±1,460 to 12,700±2,980 cells/mm3, P<0.05), neutrophilia (PMNs 1,825±280 to 4,055±225 cells/mm3, P<0.05), increased activated NBT+ PMNs (220±218 to 609±635 cells/mm3, P<0.05), and when subsequently subjected to hemorrhagic shock resulted in 100% mortality (0/6 survival).

claim: Support is partially established in this source. Staubach et al. (1998) report that 51 surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis/septic shock were randomized within 12 hours of diagnosis to receive continuous IV pentoxifylline 1 mg/kg/hour (max 1800 mg/day) or placebo (saline) for up to 28 days (or until ICU discharge or death). The study reports no significant between-group differences over the study in serum endotoxin (LPS) and TNF-α/IL-6 bioactivity, nor in bilirubin, creatinine, or platelet count, and no significant differences in 28-day or in-hospital survival (log-rank P=.85 and P=.43, respectively). The MOD score decreased from day 4 onward in the pentoxifylline group vs placebo, reaching statistical significance on day 14 (P<.05; Student t test with Bonferroni correction). PaO2/FiO2 was significantly improved on days 14 and 17 (P<.05), and pressure-adjusted heart rate was significantly improved on day 6 (P<.05). Table 2 supports baseline (enrollment) comparability, not longitudinal 'no differences' claims; this source does not provide Table-based day-by-day P-values for those lab measures.
source_text:
**Patients:** Fifty-one surgical patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline continuously (27 patients) or saline infusion as placebo (24 patients).

**Interventions:** Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.

Fifty-one surgical patients were randomly assigned within 12 hours after diagnosis of sepsis to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (Rentyllin, Rentschler, Germany) 1 mg/kg of body weight per hour, to a maximum of 1800 mg/d or normal saline solution as placebo during 28 days or until patients were discharged from the ICU or died.

The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in patients receiving pentoxifylline and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group. In-hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 54% (13/24) in the placebo group (**Figure 1**). There were no significant differences in the survival curves of the groups (log-rank analysis,  $P=.85$  for 28-day survival and  $P=.43$  for hospital survival).

At baseline, the multiple organ dysfunction score was not different between the groups. From day 4 after the diagnosis of sepsis, the score decreased in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with placebo-infused patients (**Figure 2**). This difference reached significance on day 14 after the diagnosis of sepsis ( $P<.05$ ). The  $\text{PaO}_2/\text{FiO}_2$  ratio as a parameter for pulmonary dysfunction increased from day 7 in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with patients receiving placebo (**Figure 3**). The difference was statistically significant on days 14 and 17 after the diagnosis of severe sepsis ( $P<.05$ ).

The pressure-adjusted heart rate characterizing cardiac function was significantly different on day 6 after diagnosis (*P*<.05) and remained decreased compared with the placebo group (**Figure 4**). The total bilirubin as a measure of hepatic dysfunction, serum creatinine as a measure of renal dysfunction, and the platelet count as a measure of hematologic dysfunction showed no differences throughout the evaluation. The serum endotoxin concentrations and IL-6 and TNF-α bioactivity were not significantly different in the groups during the study.

**Figure 2.** *Serial multiple organ dysfunction (MOD) score according to Marshall... Asterisk indicates* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline (solid bars) vs patients receiving placebo (shaded bars); Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction.*

**Figure 3.** *Changes in  $\mathrm{PaO_2/FIO_2}$  (fraction of inspired oxygen) ratio... Asterisks indicate* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline... vs patients receiving placebo...; Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction.*

**Figure 4.** *Changes in pressure-adjusted heart rate... Asterisk indicates* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline... vs patients receiving placebo...; Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction.*
verdict_explanation: Correct on: population size and allocation (27 vs 24), setting (surgical ICU), severe sepsis/septic shock; dosing (1 mg/kg/h; max 1800 mg/d), duration (up to 28 days), and timing (randomized within 12 hours of diagnosis); mortality numerators/denominators and log-rank P-values; and which days showed P<.05 for MODS (day 14), PaO2/FiO2 (days 14 and 17), and PAHR (day 6), including use of Student t test with Bonferroni correction (as stated in figure captions and Statistical Analysis). Not fully correct: attributing the 'no significant differences' lab/organ-function findings specifically to 'Table 2' across the study. Table 2 reports enrollment (baseline) values only; the text (not Table 2) states that bilirubin/creatinine/platelets and endotoxin/cytokine bioactivity were not significantly different between groups during the study. Also, the source refers to "tumor necrosis factor α" and "interleukin 6 bioactivity" and does not mention 'serum TNF-α/IL-6' beyond bioactivity; and it reports PaO2/FiO2 significance on days 14 and 17 (not day 14 and 17 plus other unspecified later days).
readiness_reason: A repaired claim is fully supportable from this source when corrected to (a) cite Table 2 only for enrollment comparability and (b) cite the Results narrative/Figures for longitudinal 'no differences' and significant-day findings.
original_claim: In 51 surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis/septic shock, PTX as continuous IV infusion (1 mg/kg/hour; max 1,800 mg/day) initiated within 12 hours of diagnosis and continued up to 28 days showed no significant differences versus placebo in serum endotoxin, TNF-α bioactivity, IL-6 bioactivity, platelet count, creatinine, or bilirubin (Table 2), and no difference in 28-day mortality (30% [8/27] vs 33% [8/24], log-rank P=.85) or in-hospital mortality (41% [11/27] vs 54% [13/24], log-rank P=.43), while MODS decreased from day 4 onward with a statistically significant reduction at day 14 and selected physiologic indices improved on certain later days (PaO2/FiO2 on days 14 and 17; PAHR on day 6; P<.05).

claim: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 51 surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis (pentoxifylline n=27; placebo n=24), patients assigned to pentoxifylline received a continuous IV infusion of 1 mg/kg body weight per hour (maximum 1800 mg/day) for 28 days or until ICU discharge or death. The median serum concentration of pentoxifylline was 3628 ng/mL on day 1 after starting infusion and 1620 ng/mL on day 2; it reached a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study. The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group; survival did not differ significantly between groups (log-rank P=.85 for 28-day survival).
source_text:
**Patients:** Fifty-one surgical patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline continuously (27 patients) or saline infusion as placebo (24 patients).

**Interventions:** Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.

Fifty-one surgical patients were randomly assigned within 12 hours after diagnosis of sepsis to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (Rentyllin, Rentschler, Germany) 1 mg/kg of body weight per hour, to a maximum of 1800 mg/d or normal saline solution as placebo during 28 days or until patients were discharged from the ICU or died.

The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in patients receiving pentoxifylline and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group. In-hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 54% (13/24) in the placebo group (**Figure 1**). There were no significant differences in the survival curves of the groups (log-rank analysis,  $P=.85$  for 28-day survival and  $P=.43$  for hospital survival).

**Figure 1.** *Kaplan-Meier 28-day survival (top) and Kaplan-Meier hospital survival (bottom) analysis for all patients assigned to receive pentoxifylline (solid squares) or placebo (open squares). Survival did not differ significantly between patient groups (*P *= .85 for 28-day survival and* P *= .43 for hospital survival).*

The median serum concentration of pentoxifylline was 3628 ng/mL on the first day after starting infusion and 1620 ng/mL on day 2; it reached a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study. A similar pattern was demonstrated for the first metabolite of pentoxifylline (BL 194) with a 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher serum concentration than the parent drug (**Figure 5**).
verdict_explanation: Dosing, N=51 with group sizes (27 vs 24), day 1 and day 2 median serum pentoxifylline concentrations (3628 ng/mL; 1620 ng/mL), and the statement that steady state was reached from day 3 through the end of the 28-day study are supported. The 28-day mortality counts/percentages and log-rank P=.85 for 28-day survival are also supported. However, the candidate adds unit conversions to µmol/L ("13.04 µmol/L"; "5.82 µmol/L"), which are not stated in the provided source text; therefore that portion is unsupported by this source.
readiness_reason: After removing unsupported µmol/L conversions, the remaining claim is directly supported by explicit statements in the source text with clear locators and quotations (study design/population, dosing, serum concentrations/steady state, and mortality with P value).
original_claim: In 51 surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis receiving continuous IV PTX at 1 mg/kg/hour (max 1800 mg/day) for up to 28 days, median serum parent PTX concentrations were reported as 3628 ng/mL (13.04 μmol/L) on Day 1 and 1620 ng/mL (5.82 μmol/L) on Day 2 with steady state from Day 3–28, while 28-day mortality was 30% (8/27) with PTX vs 33% (8/24) with placebo (P=.85).

source_text:
Results: "Fifteen patients had severe hypocortisolism after TSS (morning plasma cortisol, <2 µg/dL). They all experienced anorexia, fatigue, somnolence of variable degree, and nausea by postoperative day 4. These symptoms were ameliorated

after the first dose of glucocorticoid replacement."
verdict_explanation: Numeric values and P-values for IL-6 and temperature across Pre-op, Postop D4–5, and Postop D9–10 are correctly reported from Table 2 (including IL-6 P<0.0001 vs pre-op at D4–5 and IL-6 P<0.0005 vs pre-op at D9–10; temperature values and significance are also supported). Protocol details are supported for the hypocortisolism threshold (<2 µg/dL), sampling time (0600–0700), and that D9–10 blood was drawn before glucocorticoid administration (24 h after last dose). Symptom cluster timing is supported (by postoperative day 4; ameliorated after first replacement dose). However, the candidate’s statement "after starting oral glucocorticoid replacement" is not fully reliable as written because the protocol specifies starting oral dexamethasone on postoperative day 5, while the Results text also says patients were placed on hydrocortisone replacement by days 9–10; the source does not cleanly and consistently specify that D9–10 corresponds specifically to "after starting oral" replacement in the exact manner claimed, and it contains an internal inconsistency regarding the replacement agent (dexamethasone vs hydrocortisone).

citation.locator: ## Diagnosis of MCAS (incl. Fig. 1; paragraphs beginning 'MCAS may be diagnosed...' through 'Thirdly, the MCAS diagnosis requires...')

claim: Gulen2024_MCAS.md states that an MCAS diagnosis is confirmed only when all three diagnostic criteria are fulfilled: (1) typical, severe, episodic mast cell activation symptoms in ≥2 organ systems; (2) laboratory evidence of an event-related, substantial transient increase in a validated mast cell activation marker during the symptomatic event compared with the patient’s baseline (with tryptase described as the gold-standard marker, and the event-related tryptase threshold given as > (sBT * 1.2 + 2) ng/mL); and (3) symptom control/response with mast cell mediator–targeting drugs. It also states that for urinary mediator metabolites (histamine, PGD2, leukotrienes), sensitivity/specificity and reliable cutoffs are not established, but it has been suggested to consider levels higher than 30% above the upper limit of normal as pathologic.
source_text:
MCAS may be diagnosed when the symptoms of MC activation are systemic (involving more than one organ system), severe, and recurrent and the MCAS criteria are fulfilled [17••, 18••]. There are three sets of criteria required for an MCAS diagnosis as illustrated in Fig. 1: (1) the presence of typical, severe, episodic MC activation symptoms in  $\geq 2$  organ systems; (2) the detection of a substantial transient increase in a validated marker of MC activation during the symptomatic event; (3) the control of symptoms with MC mediator–targeting drugs.

The clinical criterion of MCAS requires the simultaneous involvement of  $\geq 2$  organ systems [17••, 18••].

Secondly, the diagnosis of MCAS requires laboratory proof. Hence, the clinical symptoms of MCAS are associated with an acute, substantial increase in the levels of a validated mediator of systemic MC activation during an episode, either in serum or urine, compared with the patient's baseline levels.

Currently, tryptase is the most MC-specific mediator that best fulfills the laboratory criterion and is used as a gold standard to document MC activation [20–22].

To diagnose MCAS, the event-related tryptase should be greater than  $\text{sBT} * 1.2 + 2$  ng/mL to confirm the clinical suspicion of MC activation, i.e., typical clinical symptoms of anaphylaxis are also present [17••, 18••, 19•].

**Fig. 1** Diagnostic criteria for mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS). All three criteria must be fulfilled to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS: **A** clinical criterion, **B** laboratory criterion; **C** response criterion.

Mediators other than tryptase, including urinary metabolites of histamine, prostaglandin D2 (PGD2), and leukotrienes, are also available but less specific for MCs and MCAS [28, 29, 30••]. Additionally, the sensitivity and specificity of these markers have not been determined, nor have the reliable indicators of systemic MC activation, such as significant increase and cut-off levels. However, recently, it has been suggested to consider levels higher than 30% above the upper limit of normal as pathologic [18••, 30••].

Thirdly, the MCAS diagnosis requires a favorable response to agents that act as MC stabilizers or inhibitors of MC mediators, such as histamine receptor antagonists (H1- and H2-antihistamines), leukotriene blockers, MC stabilizers, and aspirin or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs) [15•, 58, 59•].

Hence, all above-mentioned three criteria should be fulfilled to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS.
verdict_explanation: The source clearly supports that all three criteria must be fulfilled (including explicit statements in Fig. 1 caption and the sentence 'Hence, all above-mentioned three criteria should be fulfilled to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS.'). It supports the tryptase diagnostic equation as written (> sBT*1.2 + 2 ng/mL) and describes tryptase as the gold standard. It also supports that urinary mediator metabolite cutoffs are not established and that it has been suggested to consider levels >30% above the upper limit of normal as pathologic (i.e., threshold is relative to ULN, not baseline). However, the candidate claim adds unsupported specifics: it asserts serum tryptase is measured '1–4 hours post-event' (the text says tryptase 'peaks in serum about 1 h after clinical onset' and discusses half-life/elevation duration but does not state a 1–4 hour sampling window), and it states urinary metabolites are 'suggested to rise substantially during flares' framed as an event-linked rise vs baseline; the quoted suggestion is specifically 'higher than 30% above the upper limit of normal' and is not framed as a flare-vs-baseline requirement in this section.
readiness_reason: The repaired claim is directly supported by exact source quotations with clear locators, and the unsupported timing detail (1–4 hours) and baseline-vs-ULN ambiguity for urinary metabolites have been removed/clarified.
original_claim: Gulen2024_MCAS.md states that confirming mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) requires simultaneous fulfillment of three consensus criteria: (1) severe, recurrent, acute episodic systemic symptoms involving ≥2 organ systems; (2) an event-linked transient elevation of a validated mast-cell activation biomarker during an acute flare vs the patient’s baseline—gold standard serum total tryptase measured 1–4 hours post-event exceeding (baseline tryptase×1.2)+2 ng/mL, and urinary mediator metabolites during flares suggested to rise substantially (e.g., >30% above the upper limit of normal); and (3) substantial clinical response/symptom control with targeted mast-cell anti-mediator therapy.

claim: Methods: Rats were divided into three groups (eight animals each); Group II underwent bilateral renal pedicle clamping for 30 min followed by 24 h reperfusion; Group III received PTX 4 mg/rat/day (20 mg/kg/day) intraperitoneally for 3 days before undergoing the same ischemia–reperfusion procedure.
source_text:
Twenty-four adult male albino rats weighing 150–200g were used in this study. They were housed in wire mesh cages and were given free access to a balanced diet and water. They were divided into three groups (eight animals each).

In the ischemic reperfusion (IR) group, the animals were subjected to renal ischemia induced by bilateral clamping of the renal pedicles for 30min. Then, the clamps were removed and 24-h reperfusion was started.

In the IR with PTX group, the animals received PTX (Trental or Vasotal) 4mg/rat/day (20mg/kg/day) [7] intraperitoneally for 3 days before the operation. Then, the animals underwent an ischemia reperfusion procedure as in group II.

verdict_explanation: Correct that the paper states: (a) “With oral preparations of PTX peak plasma levels are less than 5 μmol/l”, and (b) “the combined level of all active forms of the drug are unlikely to exceed 10 μmol/l.” Correct that the Abstract uses “clinically achievable concentration (5–10 μmol/l)” and that the Introduction criticizes/confounds interpretation due to prior millimolar in vitro concentrations. source_text: In 8 experiments FMLP stimulated a rapid increment in cAMP from resting levels to  $18.1 \pm 5.4$  pmol/ $10^7$  cells within 10 to 20 s of stimulation. Pre-incubation with 100 or 500  $\mu$ mol/l PTX 15 min before FMLP stimulation enhanced both the magnitude and duration of the cAMP responses (Fig. 5a) ( $p < 0.001$ ,  $n = 5$ , Students t-test). Lower concentrations of PTX between 0.5 to 50  $\mu$ mol/l did not induce these effects (Fig. 5b).
verdict_explanation: Correct on the tested concentration ranges and qualitative findings: 0.5–50 µmol/L had no effect on FMLP-stimulated cAMP response; 100/500 µmol/L enhanced the cAMP response; ≤50 µmol/L did not alter resting or stimulated Ca2+ while 500 µmol/L reduced both with p<0.05; and Discussion explicitly concludes effects at ≤50 µmol/L are unlikely due to PDE inhibition. Incorrect/unsupported specifics: the candidate's numeric cAMP change 'from ~18 to ~45 pmol/10^6 cells' conflicts with the paper's reported unit (pmol/10^7 cells) and the text does not report a ~45 pmol/10^6 doubling value for 100 and 500 µmol/L.

source_text:
**Animals**—6 healthy adult mixed-breed dogs.

On day 2, oral treatment with pentoxifylline was initiated at a dosage of 20 mg/kg (compounded into a liquid to allow precise dosing) 3 times daily. Treatment continued for 29 days (until day 30). Two hours after discontinuation of drug treatment on day 30, each dog was sedated with dexmedetomidine and again admin-

istered the intradermal injections... At 24 hours after these repeated injections (day 31)... biopsy specimens...

On day 37, the sedation and intradermal injection procedures were repeated... At 24 hours after these repeated injections (day 38)...

**Treatment with pentoxifylline**—Treatment with pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg, PO, q 8 h) was initiated on day 2 and continued until 2 hours before the dogs were sedated on day 30.

Procedures—... On day 2, treatment with pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg, PO, q 8 h) was initiated and continued until day 30. For each dog, injection, measurement, and biopsy procedures were repeated on days 30 to 31 and on days 37 to 38 (ie, after discontinuation of pentoxifylline administration).
verdict_explanation: Regimen/days (6 healthy adult dogs; pentoxifylline 20 mg/kg PO q8h/3 times daily; started day 2; continued until day 30; injections/measurements on days 30–31 and 37–38) and timepoints (20 min, 6 h, 24 h) are supported. The source reports no significant effect at 20 minutes (P>0.05) and significant reduction of the 6-hour late-phase reaction on day 30 (P<0.05) with stronger inhibition at 24 hours (day 31). At 20 hours after CLP, plasma TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 were significantly elevated in CLP animals and PTX significantly attenuated these increases; per the figure legend, CLP differs from sham (* P<0.05) and PTX differs from CLP (# P<0.05), and the text reports no statistically significant differences between PTX-treated and sham-operated animals for these cytokines.
source_text:
*Administration of PTX.* One hour after CLP, animals were re-anesthetized with methoxyflurane inhalation and the femoral vein was cannulated using PE-50 tubing. PTX (50 mg/kg body wt in 1 mL normal saline solution; Sigma, St. Louis, MO) was infused through the venous catheter at a constant infusion rate over a period of 90 min. ... 

Twenty hours after CLP (i.e., the late, hypodynamic stage of sepsis), the thoracic aorta and small intestine were isolated and precontracted by norepinephrine. Rat ADM ( $10^{-7}$  M) was applied, and the percentage of ADM-induced relaxation in the aortic rings and resistance vessels in the small intestine was determined.

**Effects of PTX on ADM-induced relaxation.** Application of ADM to vessels from sham-operated animals induced  $76.4 \pm 2.6\%$  relaxation in NE-preconstricted aortic rings (Fig. 1A) and  $94.5 \pm 2.4\%$  relaxation in intestinal vessels (Fig. 1B). Vascular responsiveness to ADM 20 h after CLP was significantly reduced in both the aortic rings ( $56.8 \pm 4.2\%$ ) and intestinal vessels ( $78.4 \pm 2.9\%$ ). However, vessels isolated from septic animals that received PTX treatment displayed no significant reduction in ADM responsiveness 20 h after CLP (aortic rings,  $73.2 \pm 5.3\%$ ; intestinal vessels,  $87.8 \pm 1.9\%$ ) as compared with vessels from sham-operated animals (Fig. 1).

**FIG. 1.** Alterations in adrenomedullin-induced vascular relaxation in aortic rings (A) and isolated small intestine (B) after sham operation, cecal ligation and puncture (CLP), or cecal ligation and puncture with pentoxifylline treatment (CLP + PTX). Values are expressed as percentages (%) of vascular relaxation following initial norepinephrine-induced vascular tension. All measurements were performed 20 h after CLP or sham operation. The data are presented as means  $\pm$  SEM and compared by ANOVA and Tukey's test.  $n = 6-8$  animals/group. \* $P < 0.05$  versus Sham group; # $P < 0.05$  versus CLP group.

**Effects of PTX on plasma ADM and inflammatory cytokines.** ... Plasma levels of TNF- $\alpha$ , IL-1 $\beta$ , and IL-6 were all significantly elevated 20 h after the onset of sepsis. However, treatment with PTX significantly attenuated the increase in inflammatory cytokines in septic animals (Fig. 3). Although the plasma cytokine levels in PTX-treated animals were slightly elevated when compared with those of sham-operated animals, there were no statistically significant differences between these two groups (Fig. 3).

**FIG. 3.** Alterations in plasma tumor necrosis factor  $\alpha$  (TNF- $\alpha$ ) (A), interleukin-1 $\beta$  (IL-1 $\beta$ ) (B), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) (C) after sham operation, cecal ligation and puncture (CLP), or cecal ligation and puncture with pentoxifylline treatment (CLP + PTX). All measurements were performed 20 h after CLP or sham operation. The data are expressed as means  $\pm$  SEM and compared by ANOVA and Tukey's test.  $n = 6-8$  animals/group. \* $P < 0.05$  versus Sham group; # $P < 0.05$  versus CLP group.

source_text:
### EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN

Six groups of animals were studied. Group 1 swine (control, n=8) received a 1-hour intravenous infusion of sterile saline solution. Group 2 swine (sepsis, n=8) received a 1-hour intravenous infusion of live *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, PAO strain (5×10^8 colony forming units per milliliter at 0.3 mL/20 kg per minute). Three further groups of animals with sepsis were studied, each receiving a 20-mg/kg bolus of pentoxifylline (Hoechst-Roussel, Somerville, NJ) followed by an infusion (6 mg/kg per hour) until the end of the experiment. Group 3 swine (pretreatment pentoxifylline, n=6) commenced the pentoxifylline regimen 15 minutes prior to the bacterial infusion. Group 4 swine (posttreatment pentoxifylline, n=6) received the bolus of pentoxifylline immediately following the termination of the bacterial infusion at 1 hour into the experiment. Group 5 swine (delayed treatment pentoxifylline, n=4) commenced pentoxifylline treatment 1 hour after the bacterial infusion for 2 hours.
verdict_explanation: Correctly reflects the model (porcine live P aeruginosa infusion), group sizes including group 5 n=4, dose (20 mg/kg bolus + 6 mg/kg per hour infusion), and timing for group 4 (at 1 hour) and group 5 (at 2 hours after onset; i.e., 1 hour after bacterial infusion ended). However: (1) pretreatment timing is 15 minutes prior (not -20 min); (2) group 5 timing phrasing in methods indicates pentoxifylline started at 2 hours after onset (1 hour after bacterial infusion for 2 hours), while the candidate claim states '+2 hours described as established septic shock'—the 'established septic shock' description is supported, but the candidate's infusion duration '(4–5 h)' is not supported as written for all groups; the paper says infusion continued until end of experiment for groups 3-4, and for group 5 'for 2 hours'; (3) mortality timing: paper says neither animal survived beyond 3 hours and also says deaths occurred within 1 hour of onset of infusion, but does NOT state 'within 1 hour of starting PTX infusion' in RESULTS (that timing is stated in COMMENT); (4) the paper does not provide the candidate's specific cardiac index values (~5.2, ~4.8, ~3.1 L/min/m^2) anywhere in the supplied text; and (5) the claim that groups 1–4 had 100% 5-hour survival is not stated in the paper excerpt; the paper only explicitly discusses group-5 mortality and notes that the model 'rarely suffer any mortality within 5 hours' (discussion Q&A). The PAP point about posttreatment not preventing the early PAP elevation is supported by Figure 1 values (0.5 h: 45 mm Hg in septic and posttreatment). BAL protein and PaO2 approximate values at 5 h are generally consistent with Figure 3 and Table 1, but the candidate's exact PaO2 numbers (~160/~140/~80) do not match the Table 1 5-hour values (164, 154, 87).

### Experimental protocol
... The PTX group (seven dogs) received PTX ... as an intravenous bolus of 20 mg/kg ... followed by a continuous infusion of 20 mg/kg·h ... until the end of the study. ... each dog received a slow intravenous bolus of 2 mg/kg of Escherichia coli endotoxin ... and followed by a saline infusion at 20 ml/kg·h throughout the study. ...

The 'no significant differences' language for the biopsy-derived measures is supported, and the cardiac-limitation hypothesis is supported (authors hypothesize persistent cardiac dysfunction limiting blood supply; they also link low oxygen pulse to limited exercise cardiac output). However, the source does not provide or describe a '19.5% reduction' in VO2peak; it reports a patient/control ratio of 0.80 (~20% lower). Also, biopsy participation was 13 matched pairs with varying usable N by assay (Table 4 N=7–8; Table 5 N=7–8), so stating a single biopsy subset size of '8 matched pairs' as a blanket description is inaccurate without qualification. The candidate’s specific list 'microvascular eNOS/NOX2-related proteins' is generally supported, but Table 5 includes additional measurements (e.g., membrane-specific NOX2) and reports ratios not always ≈1.0 (e.g., eNOS protein content P/C ratio 1.14).

original_claim: Roerink et al. (2019) report that patients in long-term remission from Cushing’s syndrome had lower exercise capacity than matched controls (VO2peak 28.0±7.0 vs 34.8±7.9 mL O2/kg/min, P<0.01; described as a 19.5% reduction), as well as lower maximal workload (176±49 vs 212±67 W, P=0.01) and lower oxygen pulse (12.0±3.7 vs 14.8±4.2 mL/beat, P=0.01). source_text:
**Animals**—6 healthy adult mixed-breed dogs.

**Procedures**—Intradermal injections (0.1 mL each) of PBS solution, histamine phosphate, and cross-linking rabbit-origin anti-canine IgE antibodies (3 injections/dog) were administered at 0 hours on day 0; wheal sizes were evaluated at 20 minutes, 6 hours, and 24 hours. ... On day 2, treatment with pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg, PO, q 8 h) was initiated and continued until day 30. For each dog, injection, measurement, and biopsy procedures were repeated on days 30 to 31 and on days 37 to 38 (ie, after discontinuation of pentoxifylline administration).

On day 2, oral treatment with pentoxifylline was initiated at a dosage of 20 mg/kg (compounded into a liquid to allow precise dosing) 3 times daily. Treatment continued for 29 days (until day 30). Two hours after discontinuation of drug treatment on day 30, each dog was sedated with dexmedetomidine and again admin-

istered the intradermal injections, as performed on day 0, this time on the right side of the thorax. Macroscopic changes were evaluated at 20 minutes and 6 hours after administration of the injections. ... At 24 hours after these repeated injections (day 31), each dog was again sedated with dexmedetomidine; macroscopic changes at the injection sites were evaluated, and biopsy specimens of noninjected skin and skin at the site of injection of anti-canine IgE antibodies were collected for histologic examination. ...

On day 37, the sedation and intradermal injection procedures were repeated for each dog on the left side of the thorax, ventral to the day 0 injection sites. Macroscopic changes were evaluated at 20 minutes and 6 hours after administration of the injections. ... At 24 hours after these repeated injections (day 38), each dog was again sedated with dexmedetomidine; macroscopic changes at the injection sites were evaluated, but biopsy specimens of skin were not collected. ...

**Grading of macroscopic reactions**—At 20 minutes, 6 hours, and 24 hours after intradermal injections were administered on days 0, 30, and 37, the injection sites were evaluated ...

**Treatment with pentoxifylline**—Treatment with pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg, PO, q 8 h) was initiated on day 2 and continued until 2 hours before the dogs were sedated on day 30.
verdict_explanation: Supported: cohort size (6), dose (20 mg/kg), route (PO), frequency (q 8 h / 3 times daily), start day (day 2), and that injections were repeated on day 30 (2 hours after discontinuation) and on day 37 (1 week after cessation), with evaluations at 20 minutes, 6 hours, and 24 hours post-injection (24-hour evaluations on days 1, 31, and 38). Not supported as written: the candidate states treatment ran 'starting Day 2 through Day 30'; the source clarifies it 'continued until 2 hours before ... day 30' / 'Treatment continued for 29 days (until day 30)' and explicitly ties discontinuation to 2 hours before sedation and repeat injections on day 30.
readiness_reason: The repaired claim is fully supported by explicit procedural text with clear timing and dosing details; remaining nuance ("until day 30" vs "until 2 hours before sedation on day 30") has been corrected.

claim: In adult male Sprague–Dawley rats subjected to polymicrobial sepsis by CLP, pentoxifylline (PTX) 50 mg/kg (in 1 mL normal saline) infused intravenously via femoral vein starting 1 h after CLP over 90 min prevented the CLP-associated reduction in adrenomedullin (ADM, 10^-7 M)-induced relaxation measured 20 h after CLP in (i) NE-preconstricted thoracic aortic rings (Sham: 76.4 ± 2.6%; CLP: 56.8 ± 4.2%; CLP+PTX: 73.2 ± 5.3%) and (ii) NE-preconstricted isolated small-intestine resistance vessels (Sham: 94.5 ± 2.4%; CLP: 78.4 ± 2.9%; CLP+PTX: 87.8 ± 1.9%). In Fig. 1, significance is indicated as * P<0.05 vs Sham and # P<0.05 vs CLP (ANOVA with Tukey’s test; n=6–8/group).
source_text:
*Administration of PTX.* One hour after CLP, animals were re-anesthetized with methoxyflurane inhalation and the femoral vein was cannulated using PE-50 tubing. PTX (50 mg/kg body wt in 1 mL normal saline solution; Sigma, St. Louis, MO) was infused through the venous catheter at a constant infusion rate over a period of 90 min. ... Vehicle-treated septic animals received 1 mL normal saline solution intravenously for 90 min. Sham-operated animals received neither PTX nor saline.

*Isolation of aortic rings and determination of ADM-induced relaxation.* ... Twenty hours after the onset of sepsis, ... When the basal tension became stable, a submaximal contraction of ~400 mg was induced by  $5 imes 10^{-9}$  M norepinephrine (Sigma). Synthetic rat ADM (Peninsula Labs, Belmont, CA) at a concentration of  $10^{-7}$  M was then applied ...

*Isolation of the small intestine and determination of ADM-induced relaxation.* ... Following a 15-min equilibration and pressure stabilization at a constant perfusion rate of 5 mL/min, blood vessels in the isolated gut were constricted with  $2.4 imes 10^{-7}$  M NE added to the buffer reservoir of the organ chamber. On pressure stabilization, synthetic rat ADM ( $10^{-7}$  M) was then applied ...

## RESULTS

**Effects of PTX on ADM-induced relaxation.** Application of ADM to vessels from sham-operated animals induced  $76.4 \pm 2.6\%$  relaxation in NE-preconstricted aortic rings (Fig. 1A) and  $94.5 \pm 2.4\%$  relaxation in intestinal vessels (Fig. 1B). Vascular responsiveness to ADM 20 h after CLP was significantly reduced in both the aortic rings ( $56.8 \pm 4.2\%$ ) and intestinal vessels ( $78.4 \pm 2.9\%$ ). However, vessels isolated from septic animals that received PTX treatment displayed no significant reduction in ADM responsiveness 20 h after CLP (aortic rings,  $73.2 \pm 5.3\%$ ; intestinal vessels,  $87.8 \pm 1.9\%$ ) as compared with vessels from sham-operated animals (Fig. 1).

**FIG. 1.** ... The data are presented as means  $\pm$  SEM and compared by ANOVA and Tukey's test.  $n = 6-8$  animals/group. \* $P < 0.05$  versus Sham group; # $P < 0.05$  versus CLP group.
verdict_explanation: Supported: animal model (adult male Sprague–Dawley rats; CLP), PTX regimen (50 mg/kg IV via femoral vein cannulation; started 1 h post-CLP; infused over 90 min), endpoint timing (measurements at 20 h after CLP), ADM concentration (10^-7 M), NE preconstriction concentrations (aorta: 5 × 10^-9 M NE; small intestine: 2.4 × 10^-7 M NE), and the exact relaxation means ± SEM for sham, CLP, and CLP+PTX in both tissues. Not supported as written: the candidate claim asserts specific pairwise P-values and comparisons (e.g., “P<0.05 vs CLP; vehicle lower than sham ... PTX P=NS vs sham”) that are not reported numerically in the RESULTS text; the paper provides only symbol-based significance definitions (* vs Sham; # vs CLP) in the Fig. 1 legend, and the RESULTS states only that PTX-treated vessels showed “no significant reduction ... as compared with ... sham-operated animals.” Also, the claim’s wording “vehicle lower than sham” is misleading for Fig. 1 because Sham animals “received neither PTX nor saline.”
readiness_reason: After removing/repairing unsupported numerical P-value details and clarifying significance reporting to the figure legend’s symbols plus the text statement about no significant reduction vs sham, the remaining claim is directly supported with explicit methods and results, including exact means ± SEM and assay conditions.
original_claim: In male Sprague-Dawley rats subjected to CLP polymicrobial sepsis, PTX given as 50 mg/kg IV femoral infusion starting 1 hour post-CLP (infused over 90 min; endpoints at 20 h) increased adrenomedullin (ADM, 10^-7 M)-induced relaxation vs CLP+vehicle in thoracic aortic rings (73.2 ± 5.3% vs 56.8 ± 4.2%; P<0.05 vs CLP; vehicle lower than sham 76.4 ± 2.6%, P<0.05 vs sham; PTX P=NS vs sham) and in small intestine resistance vessels (87.8 ± 1.9% vs 78.4 ± 2.9%; P<0.05 vs CLP; sham 94.5 ± 2.4% with vehicle P<0.05 vs sham).

source_text:
*Administration of PTX.* One hour after CLP, animals were re-anesthetized with methoxyflurane inhalation and the femoral vein was cannulated using PE-50 tubing. **Determination of plasma ADM and inflammatory cytokines.** Twenty hours after CLP or sham operation, whole blood was drawn from a femoral artery catheter into a syringe. ... Plasma levels of ADM were determined using a radioimmunoassay kit ... Plasma levels of tumor necrosis factor  $\alpha$  (TNF- $\alpha$ ), interleukin-1 $\beta$  (IL-1 $\beta$ ), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits ...

claim: In this review of BPH/LUTS pharmacotherapy in older men, the authors report that the LUTS-FORTA classification labeled silodosin and tamsulosin as “caution” due to no data on efficacy/safety in older people and risk of hypotension, especially with other anti-hypertensive medications; and labeled alfuzosin, doxazosin, and terazosin as “avoid” due to increased risk for orthostatic hypotension, vasodilatory effects, cardiac arrhythmias, and syncope.
source_text: The Fit fOR The Aged (FORTA) classification, introduced in 2008, is a classification system aimed at helping physicians in the screening process for harmful or inappropriate medications in older patients. Involving over 200 medications and 25 experts, the classification system labels medications from class A to D, with A being “absolutely,” B being “beneficial,” C being “caution,” and D being “do not or avoid” for men over 65 years old based on available research information. The FORTA classification system for medications in older adults studied the various alpha-blockers commercially available and labeled silodosin and tamsulosin as “caution” due to there being no data on efficacy and safety in older people and for their risks of hypotension, especially in the setting of other anti-hypertensive medications. It labeled alfuzosin, doxazosin, and terazosin as “avoid” due to their increased risk for orthostatic hypotension, vasodilatory effects, cardiac arrhythmias, and syncope [15••].
verdict_explanation: Supported: the review reports FORTA meanings (A–D) and states that silodosin and tamsulosin are labeled “caution” (corresponding to Class C), and that alfuzosin, doxazosin, and terazosin are labeled “avoid” (corresponding to Class D), with the stated rationales including hypotension (including orthostatic hypotension) and, for the avoid group, syncope and cardiac arrhythmias. Not supported as written: the candidate claim says the review states that “co-administration of alpha-blockers with antihypertensives increases risk of orthostatic blood pressure drops and syncope.” The source ties the antihypertensive co-medication context to “risks of hypotension” (not explicitly orthostatic hypotension or syncope) for the caution group; and it mentions syncope as part of the avoid group rationale without explicitly linking syncope to co-administration with antihypertensives.
readiness_reason: The repaired claim is directly supported by explicit statements in the provided source text, including medication-specific FORTA category terms (“caution,” “avoid”) and the stated rationales; it avoids the unsupported linkage of antihypertensive co-administration to orthostatic hypotension/syncope.
original_claim: A review of BPH/LUTS pharmacotherapy in older men states that co-administration of alpha-blockers with antihypertensives increases risk of orthostatic blood pressure drops and syncope, and reports FORTA classifications in which non-selective alpha-blockers (alfuzosin, doxazosin, terazosin) are Class D ('Avoid') due to severe orthostatic hypotension/cardiac arrhythmia risks, while selective agents (tamsulosin, silodosin) are Class C ('Caution').

PTX has potent anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and increasing the production of anti-inflammatory cytokines in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) (Fernandes et al. 2008). claim: In a monocentric, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2×2 factorial randomized trial in women with superficial radiation-induced fibrosis (RIF), participants were randomly assigned for 6 months to: (A) pentoxifylline (PTX) 800 mg/day (two 400-mg tablets) plus vitamin E (Vit E) 1,000 U/day (two 500-U capsules), (B) PTX plus placebo capsules, (C) placebo tablets plus Vit E, or (D) placebo tablets and capsules. At 6 months, mean relative RIF surface regression (index 6 months, %) was −60.2 (SD 10.7) in group A versus −42.6 (SD 17.4) in group D, with P = .038 for A vs D (Wilcoxon rank sum test). A two-way ANOVA across the four groups found no significant marginal effects and reported a trend toward an interaction between PTX and Vit E (P = .09).
source_text:
To assess the efficacy and synergism of PTX and Vit E as an antifibrotic treatment in patients with measurable areas of symptomatic chronic radiotherapy damage, we performed the present monocentric, double-blind, randomized clinical trial of combined PTX/Vit E versus placebo. A  $2 \times 2$  factorial design was used to allow testing for drug interactions and the marginal effects of each treatment.

In an individual double-blind design, the 24 women included were randomly assigned, for 6 months, to a combination of 800 mg/d of PTX in two 400-mg tablets and 1,000 U/d of Vit E in two 500-U capsules (group A), PTX and placebo capsules (group B), placebo tablets and Vit E (group C), and placebo tablets and capsules (group D).

For the main treatment comparison (A *v* D) involving the main and secondary end points, we used the Wilcoxon rank sum test. ... Two-way analyses of variance (ANOVA) were performed to test the respective marginal effects of PTX and Vit E and their interactions, resulting in a procedure that involved comparison of the four groups.

At 6 months, we observed a significant mean RIF surface regression of 60% with combined PTX/Vit E in group A, versus 43% for double placebo in group D ( $P = .038$ ). ... Two-way ANOVA for the four groups disclosed no significant effects, though there was a trend toward significance for the effect of PTX and Vit E interaction ( $P = .09$ ).

Table 3. ... Index 6 months, % ... Group A ... Mean -60.2 ... SD 10.7 ... Group D ... Mean -42.6 ... SD 17.4
verdict_explanation: All key elements are supported: monocentric double-blind 2×2 factorial randomization; 6-month duration; doses (PTX 800 mg/day; Vit E 1,000 U/day) and four groups; Table 3 provides the mean and SD for relative surface regression at 6 months (index 6 months, %) as −60.2 (SD 10.7) for PTX/Vit E vs −42.6 (SD 17.4) for double placebo; Primary Analyses reports P = .038 and a two-way ANOVA with no significant effects and an interaction trend P = .09. Minor repair: the source reports P = .038 but does not restate within Primary Analyses that this P-value is specifically from the Wilcoxon rank sum test (that test is specified in Statistical Analysis for A vs D), so the linkage is inferential but strongly implied by the described analysis plan.
readiness_reason: Claim components (design, dosing/duration, group arms, outcome definition as index %, group means/SD, and reported P-values including ANOVA interaction trend) are directly supported by verbatim text and Table 3 in the supplied source, with only a minor clarification about the test attribution for P=.038.
original_claim: In a monocentric double-blind 2x2 factorial RCT in women with superficial radiation-induced fibrosis, participants received for 6 months: PTX 800 mg/day + vitamin E 1,000 IU/day, PTX 800 mg/day + placebo, placebo + vitamin E 1,000 IU/day, or double placebo; the primary comparison reported that PTX+vitamin E produced greater mean relative RIF surface regression (−60.2% ± 10.7%) than double placebo (−42.6% ± 17.4%) with p=0.038, while a 2-way ANOVA reported no main effect for PTX alone or vitamin E alone and a trend toward interaction (p=0.09).

*Administration of PTX.* One hour after CLP, animals were re-anesthetized with methoxyflurane inhalation and the femoral vein was cannulated using PE-50 tubing. Vehicle-treated septic animals received 1 mL normal saline solution intravenously for 90 min. ...

**Effects of PTX on ADM-induced relaxation.** Application of ADM to vessels from sham-operated animals induced  $76.4 \pm 2.6\%$  relaxation in NE-preconstricted aortic rings (Fig. 1A) and  $94.5 \pm 2.4\%$  relaxation in intestinal vessels (Fig. 1B). Vascular responsiveness to ADM 20 h after CLP was significantly reduced in both the aortic rings ( $56.8 \pm 4.2\%$ ) and intestinal vessels ( $78.4 \pm 2.9\%$ ). However, vessels isolated from septic animals that received PTX treatment displayed no significant reduction in ADM responsiveness 20 h after CLP (aortic rings,  $73.2 \pm 5.3\%$ ; intestinal vessels,  $87.8 \pm 1.9\%$ ) as compared with vessels from sham-operated animals (Fig. 1).

claim: Gülen (2024) states that to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS, all three diagnostic criteria must be fulfilled: (A) typical, severe, episodic mast cell activation symptoms in ≥2 organ systems (events typically meet the clinical criteria of anaphylaxis); (B) laboratory evidence of an event-related mast-cell activation marker increase, with serum tryptase criterion given as event-related tryptase > (sBT * 1.2 + 2) ng/mL; and (C) a favorable response to mast cell mediator–targeting therapy, including H1- and H2-antihistamines, leukotriene blockers, mast cell stabilizers, and aspirin or NSAIDs.
source_text:
There are three sets of criteria required for an MCAS diagnosis as illustrated in Fig. 1: (1) the presence of typical, severe, episodic MC activation symptoms in  $\geq 2$  organ systems; (2) the detection of a substantial transient increase in a validated marker of MC activation during the symptomatic event; (3) the control of symptoms with MC mediator–targeting drugs.

The clinical criterion of MCAS requires the simultaneous involvement of  $\geq 2$  organ systems [17••, 18••]. Thus, MCAS events typically meet the clinical criteria of anaphylaxis.

To diagnose MCAS, the event-related tryptase should be greater than  $\text{sBT} * 1.2 + 2$  ng/mL to confirm the clinical suspicion of MC activation, i.e., typical clinical symptoms of anaphylaxis are also present [17••, 18••, 19•].

Thirdly, the MCAS diagnosis requires a favorable response to agents that act as MC stabilizers or inhibitors of MC mediators, such as histamine receptor antagonists (H1- and H2-antihistamines), leukotriene blockers, MC stabilizers, and aspirin or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs) [15•, 58, 59•].

**Fig. 1** Diagnostic criteria for mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS). All three criteria must be fulfilled to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS: **A** clinical criterion, **B** laboratory criterion; **C** response criterion.

claim: Staubach et al. report a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in 51 surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis randomized within 12 hours after diagnosis to continuous IV pentoxifylline 1 mg/kg/hour (maximum 1800 mg/day) (n=27) or saline placebo (n=24), administered for up to 28 days or until ICU discharge or death. Pentoxifylline serum concentrations were measured by gas-liquid chromatography; the median serum pentoxifylline concentration was 3628 ng/mL on day 1 and 1620 ng/mL on day 2, reaching a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study. The first metabolite (BL 194) showed a similar pattern and had 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher serum concentrations than parent drug. The multiple organ dysfunction score decreased from day 4 in the pentoxifylline group vs placebo and reached a significant difference on day 14 (P<.05; Student t test with Bonferroni correction). PaO2/FIO2 was significantly improved on days 14 and 17 (P<.05; Student t test with Bonferroni correction). Pressure-adjusted heart rate (PAHR) was significantly improved on day 6 (P<.05) and remained decreased compared with placebo. Survival did not differ significantly between groups (log-rank P=.85 for 28-day survival; P=.43 for hospital survival); 28-day mortality was 30% (8/27) vs 33% (8/24) and hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) vs 54% (13/24).
source_text:
**Design:** Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.

**Patients:** Fifty-one surgical patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline continuously (27 patients) or saline infusion as placebo (24 patients).

**Interventions:** Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.
